title: Makes It Super Easy to Extract, Back Up, Share Photos Stored on Mobile Devices
text:
IBI - THE SMART PHOTO MANAGER (US Version) makes it super easy to extract, back up, and share photos stored on my mobile devices. Instead of emailing cell phone photos that I want to share among electronic devices (an iPad Air (3rd Gen), a desktop PC, and a Samsung Galaxy cell phone), I can upload the photos to Ibi via a network connection with only a couple of clicks in the Ibi app.

No longer do I have to address an email, select and add the photos, send the email--and then reverse the process on a second device (open the email, download the photos, and save the photos to the device). All that’s necessary is to take the photos, open the Ibi app, choose “import photos”, select the photos, and hit the import button.

The photos are immediately uploaded to Ibi, and I can access them immediately on all of my other devices. There is no need to clutter up email or to consume precious storage space on my mobile devices, when all I want to do is share photos.

Ibi is extremely versatile. It allows you to sort and organize photos, and create Albums. It allows you to authorize certain people to email photos directly to Ibi. It allows you to set up different areas of Ibi for the use of individuals. It allows you to upload its contents to a PC or other even larger storage device by plugging in a USB cable (not included). It even allows you to stream your videos to a television set (using Chromecast or Roku apps).

Ibi is easy to set up, using Bluetooth. My iPad and my Galaxy phone both found the powered on (plugged in) Ibi in less than 30 seconds. Once set up, Ibi communicates via your home network’s Internet access. When your Ibi app is set up, click on Help, and download the complete user manual (a PDF file). The manual is easy to understand, and will enable you to get the most out of your Ibi.

Ibi is a small drive that easily fits on a bookshelf. It uses just one power cord. I really love this Ibi storage drive. It is simplifying my life.

+++++IMPORTANT NOTE: You should NOT choose “automatic backup” in the Ibi app Settings until you understand how the app works. With automatic backup enabled, Ibi will copy all of the photos stored on EACH mobile device, and you will probably get a lot of duplicate photos. For example, if you have been sharing and storing the same photos on an iPad and a cell phone, Ibi will copy the photos from each device. Worse, if you go into Ibi and delete the duplicates, Ibi will keep automatically adding the photos back as long as the photos still exist in storage on the two different devices.

You will probably want to use “automatic backup” when you first set up your Ibi. That way all of your photos will be automatically copied to Ibi to start you off. But you should turn “automatic backup” off before you start deleting duplicate photos. You will never have a problem with duplicate photos if automatic backup is turned off.+++++

title: DO NOT REMOVE home button plastic cover; case is excellent but instructions do not list this issue
text:
I just ordered this for my 7th generation iPad and the case itself appears to be almost indestructible. In fact it is so well put together that it takes about 30 minutes just to install it with the iPad.

INSTALLATION
- Pull the stand off the case.

- Remove the silicone outer rim from the cover. I found removing the silicone rim hard to figure out until I took my fingernail to peel if off the track that goes around the entire top of the case. It gets peeled off from the outermost edge.

- Unhinge the miniscule snaps (by the arrows) located around the case in order to open it. Once again, my stubby fingernails came in handy. It is only then that the iPad can be inserted.

- Insert the iPad into the open case. Make sure it is facing correctly based on the orientation of the case.

- DO NOT remove the plastic film covering the home button that is on the clear plastic case top. I did not know this and removed it and it damaged the cover with glue (see photos). It removed cleanly on all but one side where tremendous glue residue was left behind. The plastic film was partially up before I even began pulling it off and is typical of the type film I see covering watch faces, etc. so naturally I removed it as there was no mention not to in the manual.

- Re-fasten the top and "snap" it into place.

- Re-attach the silicone rim. Make sure that the rim once again is pulled up and over the top of the case and that the silicone edge is pushed into the track around the case. If it is not seated in the track, the case will not be sealed correctly.

With regard to the large smear of glue residue left behind by the thin plastic film that covered the home button. I contacted support to find out what can be used to remove this residue but there was nothing they could recommend with the iPad inside. They did say possibly hand sanitizer because it had alcohol in it but that should not touch the iPad. A damp rag did not work nor did a rag with water. This is extremely upsetting to me because it mars an otherwise nice looking case. However, they are sending me a replacement case with a possible return label for the "new" damaged case. I will update my review after I receive the new case.

The stand is detachable and has two heights that can be used in four positions. What this means is that the low stand can be used with the iPad in the portrait or landscape postion. The stand can then be reversed for standing up the iPad in the portrait or landscape postion. I personally only like the landscape position for either height as it feels like the iPad is going to fall using in portrait mode.

Also note that the stand is not easy to just snap on and off of the case if one is storing it there. It takes a little bit of effort and time. Although, it can be snapped on the case for portability, I have chosen not to do this because of this difficulty. Instead I just choose to lay the stand on top of the iPad so it is easily put into service.

In summary, this is an excellent case that offers superb protection for the iPad. The case is extremely heavy. It is almost like carrying a laptop around from the olden days. I love the low stand angle with the iPad in the landscape position; in fact, that is the only way I like the stand. This postion is perfect for typing on the iPad as if one is typing on a keyboard.  I am, however, very upset about the glue left behind from the plastic circle strip that covered the home button which I should not have removed but which was not mentioned in the manual. Had my cover not been destroyed by this glue, I would have rated this 4 stars. If there was no glue residue and the stand was part of the cover and was not so heavy, I would have rated this 5 stars. I personally prefer a stand that is attached to the case. This requires setup each time as a separate piece.

UPDATE: I updated my review above regarding the home button sticker I pulled off. Otter box said it was not supposed to get removed because it is a fully enclosed system. I asked them to update their documentation to say this so others do not make the same mistake I did. I will post another update after my new case arrives and perhaps update this review to 4 stars if it is satisfactory.

UPDATE 2/29/20 - I finally got my replacement Otter Box and it is working fine. I now know not to remove that plastic film over the Home Button even if it looks like it is falling off or should come off.

title: Better than the Strap that Came with my Camera
text:
I have come to understand the value of a good camera strap. It is more than just a designer item and more than just a simple strap to keep the camera hanging around your neck. It needs to be strong enough to keep the camera secure and it needs to be long enough to allow for grabbing the camera and taking a quick shot instead of having to struggle with getting the camera from around your neck and risk missing the shot by a second or two. The strap that came with my camera is functional but much too short and I expect it to rip eventually. This strap by Orota is a much better strap than that provided with my camera.

This is a well-made strap. One side is a heavy weave not unlike a car’s seat belt but not as smooth and shiny. It is also quite a bit thicker than a seat belt and will have no issue with supporting the camera. Sewn to it is a decorative layer that is also a heavy weave, similar to but not exactly like canvas. These are stitched together with heavy thread and I see little risk of them separating.

Each end is clamped with a leather reinforcement that is held in place with four metal rivets. The leather ends each hold a metal buckle with the thinner nylon straps that actually connect to the camera. Looking closely at each component I found no loose threads, no uneven seams, no flaws in fabric or materials. There is nothing about this strap that suggests it will fail under daily use.

This is a much longer strap than what came with my camera, measuring a little less than 3' long. I like the fact that with this trap attached to my camera I can lift my camera and quickly get the shot I want and I don’t have to take it from my neck in order to focus on it. I can hold it far enough from my face to actually focus on the camera. This is a very big improvement over my old strap which was short enough that I could not get the camera in front of my face at a comfortable distance.

This is a very well-made strap and I am very pleased with it. It is stylish, well constructed and it is long enough to make it much more useful to me than my old strap.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Not bad.
text:
Was actually pleased by the caps when they arrived. I used to be particular about keycap quality, but in the last few years the quality and cost of keycaps have been awesome; I'm so thrilled about those new to the hobby (although it's still expensive). When GMK 9009 was originally announced, I thought it was the perfect modern edition of classic beige. Everyone should have a good classic beige set, and 9009 is it.

Right now, my workhorse keyboard is a polycarbonate 910 with Cherry MX Grays and third-party springs (I forget the weight). Typing on it is a dream every day, and the keycaps can enhance the experience. I prefer PBT on this keyboard because it has a more pleasant, thocky sound than ABS caps. There's also a bit of tactile pushback with ABS, at least from what I noticed. While I love 9009, I'm not thrilled about ABS. Sure, ABS is cool and develops a nice shine based on use, but I prefer the consistent feel of PBT; having some keycaps stripped of their coating from use while others still feel new can throw me off. All that to say that I'm glad I was able to get this 9009 set in PBT. I was very hesitant, though, because the price for this many dye-sublimated, PBT keycaps was too good to be true.

When the package arrived, I was disappointed to find that there was no shipping box. The keycaps arrived in their manufacturer box with a shipping label slapped on it. Not only can that increase the chances of theft, but the shipping label covers the rendering that shows all the keycaps included. So now I'll have to resort to the listing to see what all should be in the box. However, nothing appears damaged. The keycaps come in wonderfully secure, plastic trays, three stacked on each other. There are a lot of keycaps here, so most keyboards should be covered. Of course, not everything will be perfect; for my 910, the Home cap is taller than the rest of the row, and there is no 1u Tab cap, nor a R1-height Fn cap. There's only one 1u blank keycap, which doesn't sit flush with the rest of the caps in its row. Minor gripes because I know my layout is particular.

But, again, there still is a great amount of keycaps so I'm sure most boards will be covered.

Now, as for the keycaps themselves. As I mentioned, I was very hesitant when the package arrived, but overall I'm pleasantly surprised. The keycaps are slightly thinner than enjoyPBT and BSP caps, and the stem can be a bit snug, but not too tight so that they don't come off easily. The sublimation is very good; I haven't noticed any that appear sloppy. Some num pad legends seem a bit thinner than others, but overall the legends are consistent and have that Cherry-legend appearance.

I wish there were more color options here, but for the price I can't complain. Truly, at $40, this set is an amazing bang for the buck.

title: Good Little DVD Player
text:
Well, I've had this for a week or so now. It's honestly cute just because of its size. I've had books that were bigger than this is. The power cord is just a bit over three feet, that's a hindrance. I was lucky enough there was a plug just in range but an extra foot of power cord would be better. The unit comes with a set of thin but serviceable RCA cables. I have some pro level RCA cables I obtained when I worked for a TV station, springs protecting the cables at the connectors, super heavy cable and insulation. . . and when I tried them with this DVD player the weight of the cables literally pulled the player off the antique dresser I use as a TV stand but the picture using the included cables is fine, playback is sharp & crisp. The unit has a functional set of controls on the front of the player which are sometimes missing in this modern era. The remote is a little small for my hands and the layout is a bit cramped and wonky but it works as long as you're in the fairly narrow field that the remote and device can see one another.
I've binged a few of my older DVD sets so far. The unit has a resume feature that picks up wherever you left off. Actually there's quite a decent set-up menu for the unit. Enough to get you going but not so much you need a degree in sound and electrical engineering to figure things out.
My only complaints so far have been;
1 - the device when loading or searching for tracks can be a bit loud but while watching content its whisper quiet.
2 - occasionally it reverts to turning the closed captioning on. There's a control on the remote, 2-3 clicks and its fixed.
3 - the already mentioned too short power cord.
Pluses are many. The player is supposed to be region free, I have no foreign DVDs to test this with. The small form factor means you can (within the limits of the cabling) put it almost anywhere. It easily fits under the corner of my large screen TV with room to spare. The display is orange, I don't know why. It's not attractive but it is easy to read from across the room (maybe that's why it's orange). It does have a voice reading function for people with impaired sight. It will read every control or function as you select them.
Not a complaint and not a plus. Most devices have a single LED that stays on to let you know it's in standby mode and ready to go. This unit steps things up a notch. When it's off it literally displays "OFF" on the screen for all to see.
I've been quite happy with the functionality of this unit. I have a decent DVD collection I haven't been able to watch for a while so I'm pleased to be able to watch these old favorites, Serial Experiment Lain, Robot Chicken, Wonderfalls and many others.
Edit - I received the instructions from the manufacturer and another user on setting this unit up as Region Free. I followed them, several times, reverting back to Region 1 each time. When set to Test - Region 0 (supposedly the region free setting) Region 1 discs become unplayable! See the image I posted. title: Kodak's Last Hurrah...
text:
Years ago I bought a little 2MP 3X Zoom digital camera. It was a Kodak and it took great pictures. Several years after that I won a Kodak Z650 in an online contest and flat out loved the pictures it took. So when the stars aligned and Amazon had the Kodak Z990 on sale and my gift card balance was enough to afford it I jumped at the opportunity.

I really LIKE the Kodak Z990 and I'm sad that it will probably be the last Kodak camera I ever buy...

I LIKE this camera... I almost love this camera. While my Z650 almost never came out of Auto mode I find myself accessing the PASM controls and bracketing the exposure compensation when I use this camera.

It isn't that the Z990 doesn't take great pictures. It does. It just takes a little work to get them.

The camera is hefty, weighing in at 1 LB. 5 OZ. (593g) and feels substantial. To me it feels like what a camera should. The gripping areas on the front handgrip and rear thumb rest are lightly rubberized and the non-movable ring on the lens has a sturdy ribbed rubber covering.

The controls are reasonably easy to access and use. I like that you can use either the 5-way controller (similar to a Kindle's) or the clickable toggle wheel next to the thumb rest to access and control many of the camera settings. I like having the zoom controls on a ring around the shutter button. It feels easier to use than those cameras that have this control on the back. It also requires a very light touch as with 30x total optical zoom the lens and controls are very sensitive. At first you will find yourself zooming or going wide-angle past the point you wanted but with a little practice it becomes much easier to control.

The Z990 uses AA batteries (4) which, personally, I think is great. You can, in a pinch, get replacements at any convenience store, gas station or mega-mart in the US. It also comes with a serviceable if feature free slow battery charger and four Kodak brand rechargeable NiMH batteries. I've since replaced these with a smart charger and better batteries but out of the box they're enough to get you started.

Another great addition is the Optical View Finder. This is incredibly handy when shooting outdoors in bright sunlight. The 3" LCD screen is great but in direct sun it, like all LCD screens, becomes almost impossible to see.

I've, as of the time of this review, taken a bit over a thousand images and a handful of videos with my Z990 and I've barely scratched the surface of experiencing all the features and functions it has to offer.

Some notable features are:
Two panoramic image modes. One has the camera stitching two or three images together to produce the image and the other allows you to hold the shutter button and 'sweep' the camera to produce the panoramic image.
Multiple Kodak film time emulations - Kodacolor, Kodachrome, Ektachrome, T-MAX, TRI-X as well as standard B&W and Sepia modes.
In camera HDR mode.
Multiple burst modes.
Full 1080p video in stereo.
The camera can even emulates a Photo Booth taking four images in quick succession and stitching them together.

Nothing being perfect the Z990 has a few cons I feel need to be mentioned:
The memory card is stored in the battery compartment and the battery door is one of the few things I worry about breaking on this camera. It is light plastic and not easy to close with batteries installed.
To use a USB cable to transfer images from the camera to a computer the camera needs to be powered up requiring removal of the lens cap (because the cap mounts on the body not the lens). I don't like that it needs to sit with the lens exposed for no reason.
The lens isn't threaded so you cannot use any filters with this camera.
Preview mode, where the camera shows you the last image taken, cannot be disabled on this model, you can bypass it somewhat by 1/2 pressing the shutter once the preview displays but it would have been nice to be able to turn off this feature.

In conclusion:
While the Kodak Z990 Max isn't perfect it is an affordable bridge camera that takes excellent pictures day or night with an extremely powerful zoom lens, a host of useful features and controls that can only be topped by DSLR cameras. As Kodak's last hurrah, it's a pretty good note to go out on.

title: Love this case - exactly what I wanted.
text:
This case is exactly what I wanted: extremely durable shock-absorbing (read: drop-proof) protection without screen protection. Let me qualify that statement: I did *not* want screen protection. I love the pearl eink display on my graphite Kindle Keyboard, and it now has a big brother. I do not want a screen cover, as this would greatly reduce the screen's otherwise remarkable clarity, adding unwanted elements such as bubbles, surface scratches, and glare to the mix--no thank you. There is a reason I disliked reading on the iPad so much I gave it back (very reflective!). In fact, this OtterBox defender case came with a stick-on screen protector--no way. It would ruin that big, glorious pearl eink display.

A screen cover serves no purpose once you remove the device from your backpack/messenger/tote/briefcase for use. Assuming you transport your Kindle device safely in an appropriate sleeve (you put your other expensive electronic equipment--your laptop/tablet in one; your Kindle deserves the same amount of respect), the screen protector is completely unnecessary--the sleeve protects the screen during travel. THAT is when the screen needs protecting--when you are not using it, from the other goodies in your messenger bag/backpack (keys, pens, earbuds, and anything else rattling around in there). Yes, that's right--I'm talking about a Kindle in an Otterbox Inside a sleeve inside your briefcase. ...Inception-level protection. You got it. Better safe than sorry, right? What if they once again stop producing our beloved Kindle DX and something happens to yours? I do not want to have to replace my DX--especially if it has to be with a Fire device (5% the battery life, reflective, heavy, expensive--no thanks!). When you are holding your Kindle in your hand, reading, a screen cover only detracts from the experience.

What you see in my pictures is exactly what you get: a beefy, black rubber (not silicone--too easily torn; rubber is much stronger) form-fitting sleeve with an equally form-fitting outer plastic shell. Science geeks like me understand how this works, and just in case you are not one, here is the idea: if you drop your device onto the floor, the outer shell absorbs some of the impact energy generated by the device hitting the floor. It then disburses the remaining energy of the impact broadly into the rubber inner lining. The rubber lining then in turn disburses the now greatly-reduced impact energy into the device. In other words, by the time the force of the impact is filtered through two layers of protection, the second of which is very absorbent and resilient (rubber) the device inside absorbs little if anything of the original impact.

I feel very good about having my Kindle DX in an Otterbox Commuter. If I ever had one of those incredibly poorly-designed (read: seriously fragile) apple devices, such as an iPad or iPhone (which I do not, and am not ever likely to), it too would live in an OtterBox Commuter case. OtterBox = the best protection a device can get. I paid $18 including shipping for this. A great price, and worth much more in terms of peace of mind.

title: Beautiful music, crisp television, immersive movies. Some Alexa functions missing
text:
There's a lot to love here with the Bose 500. We have a Denon Soundbase w/ Bluetooth Streaming Audio in our master bedroom and a Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System in the living room - both are from 2015. I'm replacing the Denon unit with this Bose 500 for several reasons, but primarily for significantly better sound quality and Alexa integration.

This is connected to a 2014 Samsung smart TV via the HDMI port. I had no issues connecting the sound bar to the Bose Music app (be sure you get the correct app from Google Play). Next you find the sound bar with the Alexa app and link your Alexa account to this machine. All I had to do for tv sound was turn off the TV speakers through the tv settings and press the tv image button on the Bose remote. Be sure to have 2 AAA batteries on hand because they don't include them for the remote.

You plug in the included headband and use the app to fully calibrate the best sound in your room by sitting in five different locations and letting the headband and sound bar talk. This takes about 6 minutes and it's definitely a step worth doing. The sound from this Bose is amazing - playing Beethoven or Hand Zimmer's soundtrack from Hannibal is immersive and gorgeous. The television is equally good - you can use the app to set the tv sound to dialogue centric for a talk show or regular for movies. You can also adjust the settings for the sound to increase/decrease bass and treble and to move more to the center or sides of the projection speakers. Once you get it set up exactly to your preferences, it can feel like a movie theater without the volume blasting you away. I'm especially loving rewatching Firefly with the Bose 500. The app also let's you do 6 preset favorite music streaming stations from Tune In, Amazon, Spotify and another service.

As to the Alexa functionality... This is actually pretty good with two glaring faults. The sound bar is always listening for the wake word like the Echos do and there's a privacy button as well. I have noticed a tiny lag on a few requests, but it's not constant. I've been getting a weird message telling me that this unit is not compatible with my Alexa routines, then it performs the routine perfectly. (For example, I say good morning and Alexa turns on our bathroom lights, the bedside lamps and gives me the weather) It's a bizarre glitch, but as long as the routines are completed, I don't care.

The first real problem is this unit cannot link to your other Echo units in a music everywhere group - I'm not sure if that's a Bose issue or an Amazon proprietary issue because our Harmon Kardon Alexa speaker cannot be linked either. This is a shame, but not a deal breaker for me, but it's still an issue. The thing that does aggravate me is that this unit is unable to connect to and read my Audible audio books. I get a message that says it is not compatible with Audible at this time. The work around is simply to use Bluetooth and stream my book via my phone or tablet. That's ridiculous with Alexa integrated into the sound bar. This may not bother anyone else, but I listen to audiobooks more than I read now and having that full body, room filling crisp audio is a great thing.

Bottom line for us is that we love this sound bar for television viewing and music. It's sleek and modern and just does it's job. In some ways, the Alexa integration isn't complete, but the basics are there for most functions. It's definitely an improvement over the old Denon box we used to have and it's even better than the Bose Solo 15 in our living room.

title: High quality NVR, but requires some trial and errors if you're not fluent in networking...
text:
THE GOOD:
--------------
* Terrific build quality. I've seen cheap ones that come to you with dented cases, and the internal circuitry looks like a half baked job with messy wires and bad soldering jobs. This is a real professional NVR.
* 4TB Hard Drive is included, but you can install a 10TB drive if you wish. That's the max capacity.
* Records 4k video, and 8MP images.
* Instant feed, no delay like wireless cams.
* App works well provided you have everything set-up properly.
* If you're not sure of what you're doing, like I was, it's easy to restore the HD back to factory default again. I had to trial and error many times, and the good thing was that he factory reset was very quick each time. It's basically like restarting the device.

THE BAD:
------------
* No cameras provided, but you knew that when you bought it.
* Manual font is for little ants to read. But it's readable. It's just my pet peeve when manufactures make it uncomfortably small.
* Just like any other network product, the manual doesn't spend anytime with what to do if your service provider goes by 192.168.254.XXX versus providers that use 192.168.1.XXX. A lot of network products go by 192.168.1, and so I get a lot of headaches being a Frontier customer. Granted I'm not fluent in networking. A networking expert reading this might say, "easy, all you have to do is this, this and this..." Well, you see, that's what I was hoping the manual would do. LOL!

Having said that... I actually got everything to work properly. I don't know how, but I did it. As mentioned above, I'm with Frontier and they use 192.168.254.xxx, so depending on how I hook up the NVR to my network, the DHCP will generate a proper working address, or it may not. Here are some noteworthy things I discovered. This pertains to my personal network/situation, but if you find yourself in the same boat, maybe this info could be useful:

1.) Connecting the NVR directly to my frontier router causes the NVR to use it's default IP address 192.168.1.XXX. This is fine if I'm viewing the cams on my ethernet connected PC. But the app over wi-fi will not work. It will say my NVR is offline.
2.) For some reason, using a POE SWITCH between my NVR and my Router makes all the features work properly. I can view on my PC, and I can view on my APP via wi-fi. So if any of these issues sounds familiar to you, then this is what worked for me... Connect the UPLINK port of the POE SWITCH to a port on the home router. Then, connect an ethernet cable from the Network port of the NVR to any of the POE ports on the POE Switch. Once I hooked it this way, the NVR's DHCP created an IP address that is in line with my Frontier network 192.168.254.xxx. Now I can view the cams on my ethernet PC, as well as my wi-fi app.
3.) Ideally, you want to connect all POE cameras directly to the NVR which has 8 ports, but if for whatever reason, you need to connect a camera to the POE SWITCH, then understand that it'll require 2 ports of the POE Switch, one for the camera and one going back to any 1 of the 8 ports on the NVR. And remember in step #2, one of the POE port is already connected to the network port of the NVR. So 3 ports total have been taken up in this scenario.

Love the quality of the hardware, as well as the streams. I also attached a screenshot of the App's live view page. You'll see I tested 2 cameras. You simply tap a camera to get the full screen view of it. I'll rate this NVR 4-Stars overall.
label: real

title: High quality poe NVR system with 4tb pre-installed, plug and play if connecting directly to NVR...
text:
[[VIDEOID:1190b451faf9653857f6725f71e2a33c]] THE GOOD:
--------------
* This is the real deal! Every component is high quality, and the NVR unit is externally and internally immaculate. Why do I have to even say this? Because I've tried other NVR systems. I have encountered NVRs with flimsy dented cases, and messy soldering jobs on the motherboard.
* 4TB is pre-installed.
* You get 8 POE cameras! A mistake I made as a newbie was thinking all I have to do is get POE switches, then I would be able to get rid of power adapters for any camera. That is incorrect! A camera has to be designated as a POE camera in order to use POE switches and POE NVRs.
* You get eight 65 ft ethernet cable. If you can run those cables back to the NVR, which has 8 ports in the back, then you won't need to hook up any intermediary POE switches. I plan to use at most four cameras, so If I need to hook up a POE switch, the four extra cables will come in handy. However, more on this issue later.
* Included are also outdoor plugs to protect your wire connections.
* PLUG & PLAY... As long as you run the ethernet cable back to the Ethernet ports of the NVR, it is plug and play. If for any reason, you need to find the IP in your service provider's router admin, look for HEROSPEED DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY. That's the name it shows up under.
* Unlike most security cameras, the live feed of this NVR system has no delay, it's real time, or pretty close to it.
* If you're using a KVM switch at your computer, so you can switch back and forth between different sources... I said in my video that once I get a USB cable to link up the KVM switch with the NVR, then I should be able to use my PC's mouse and keyboard, which are connected to the KVM switch. Well, since then I've learned that what I said is half true. I'll be able to use the mouse, but not the keyboard. The NVR doesn't respond to any keyboards no matter if it's through the KVM switch, or directly connected to the NVR. It only uses the onscreen pop-up. You will need to use the mouse to select the letters and numbers from the virtual keyboard.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Like I said above, it's plug and play as long as you connect each camera directly back to the NVR ports. It goes without saying, but the NVR also needs to be connected to your router or nearby switch to be online. I'm running into issues testing POE switches. If the camera is not directly connected to the back of the NVR, the system cannot find it. There are 16 channels available in the NVR, and only 8 ports in the back, so obviously, this should be compatible with POE switches. But so far, I can't get it to work. I've asked for help from OSI, so we'll see...
* No guidance or instructions on how to install the actual cameras. For a moment, I was SMH. I was looking for the bases. I thought my package was missing them. But I realized the bases were already threaded onto the cameras. For each camera, you need to unthread the base, drill the base onto the ceiling of your choice location, then thread the main camera body back on it.
* Another nitpick is that installing under a ceiling will not always be ideal, or possible. It would have been great if they had included some adapters so that we can install them onto walls like bullet cameras.

Despite the little nitpicks, I still rate this 4-Stars right now. Might bump it up to 5-Stars if we can get the POE switches sorted out. I'm a newbie, so I know this might be easy for experienced networkers. The manual is a bit lacking. There were no discussions on how to install the cameras, and it assumes you'll be directly connecting all cameras back to the NVR, so it doesn't discuss the use of POE switches at all.

title: A terrific photo box, but you'll need to clear your living room to put this thing together...
text:
SEPTEMBER 23, 2021 UPDATE:
------------------------------------
* Loving this thing more and more every day. But I wanted to discuss a little more about the floor space that you'll need to assemble at home. I listed this as a "bad" in my initial review. Recently, I was able to dismantle it and reassemble it in my garage. You have to dismantle because a 40 inch square isn't going to fit through any of your doors. I absolutely did not have 13.3 ft by10 ft worth of empty space in my garage to lay down the material that covers the frame. But because I am now familiar with the material, the orientation of it, where it zips up, etc... I was able to just let the material sit all bunched up. I then rebuilt the frame inside the material. It was a bit funny cause I'm working inside out, a 40 inch square is huge, I found myself inside the frame zipping the material up from the inside. It's a weird scene if you were to walk in on me. LOL! So it is possible for you to do the same, you don't need to clear a 13.3 ft by 10 ft floor space. However, do follow my advice in setting up the backdrop last. Please read the original review below.

ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW:
-------------------------------

THE GOOD:
--------------
* Led lights provided are very bright. That's also due to the fact that you're trapping light in a box with reflector material on all sides.
* Assembly isn't difficult to understand at all, it is easy. But more on this in the BAD section.
* You get a carrying bag as well as 5 pvc color backgrounds.
* 40" square shooting space is huge!!!
* 3 types of shooting angles, depending on how much light you want to trap.

THE BAD:
------------
* A little QC issue... My led light came with a broken clip, and instead of bothering the seller since the light still worked, I just used sugru to mold a new clip.
* Think long and hard if you need this 40 inch version. There are smaller versions. It can be unwieldy to handle this 40 inch version. Like I said above, it's not difficult to understand how to put it together. It's just you need a lot of space. It doesn't come to you in a square form. You first build the 40 inch square pvc frame. Then you lay the main material that makes the box on your floor, you put the frame on it, then you fold it up, wrapping it around the pvc frame and zip everything up. It isn't difficult at all, the problem is the floor space you'll need! 13.3 x 10 ft worth of empty floor space to lay the material down. For some people, especially people with kids, it is not easy to find this much open floor space. LOL! I included a picture from the manual to show you what I'm trying to articulate.

MOST IMPORTANT TIP:
---------------------------
* Don't follow the instructions in laying the background on the floor, and then putting the frame on it. If you do it this way, you'll never change backgrounds again because it is a hassle. Secondly, the background will then be under the frame, so the back bottom frame will be exposed in the pictures. What you should do is follow the instructions, except for the background part, just leave it out. Then when everything is done. Choose the background you want. It has velcro on both upper left and right corners. Inside your box will have the velcro counterpart on both the upper left and right corners as well. So you simply stick your background on it. It is pvc and doesn't crease easily, you can bend and curve it at the bottom to achieve a seamless look with the frame hidden underneath. Not only will your pictures be nicer without the exposed frame, but if you change your mind about the color, swapping the background will be much easier too. Here is an example of product pictures I took for another Amazon review using this light box. https://www.amazon.com/review/R3FM8X6Z2ZFY7E/ref=cm_cr_srp_d_rdp_perm?ie=UTF8

I'll rate this 4-Stars! It would be 5-Stars if not for the QC issue.

3. A usb-c to usb-c cable. To connect from the Qubii to the usb-c port of your Android phone.

* This is a good idea, now that Google Photos is no longer unlimited.

* Every time you want to transfer files to your PC, NAS, etc., you'll need to remove the micro sd card if your pc doesn't have a usb-c port. My PC does not, so I use a usb to usb-c adapter. This eliminates the hassle of having to take out micro sd cards, dealing with card readers, etc.
* After you transfer everything safely to your pc, if you delete the files on the micro SD card to clear space, the Qubii still maintains its count. So even if these files are still on your phone, it will not re-download them again.

In conclusion, how accurate and precise this system is remains to be seen. So far, it has backed up everything I need it to. title: Nifty tech with a lot of quirks that you have to get used to...
text:
THE GOOD:
--------------
* It will do as it says.. capture videos from your sources.
* Video quality seems fine to me. I'm not that picky, the stuff I record isn't important.
* You can install a micro SD card, or connect a hard drive via usb.

THE BAD:
-----------
* Consistent with their products, they cut corners when it comes to the remote control. It's just a terrible clunky experience. I can't even put into words what's wrong with it. I guess there is a delay. So if you're impatient, you'll be pressing too many buttons, and you'll be in the wrong menu, navigate to the wrong places, enable the wrong features, etc. So my advice is to be patient. Press the button you want to press, then wait a week for it to respond. I don't know what inner components make a great remote control. Whatever they are, they are not inside ClearClick remotes. I've reviewed some of their other Clearclick products that are $150 and less, and so I was more forgiving. But at $250, really? You're going to still skimp out on the remote at this price range?

* If you toggle into PLAYBACK mode... good luck getting out of it. Back button doesn't work, and it's always thinking you want to delete files. Everytime I escape playback mode, I'm relieved, but also have no clue how I got out.

* Power on/off is weird. There are scenarios that will make your heart stop because you'll think the device shorted out. Just like their terrible remotes, I've noticed this power issue with their other models too. The quirk is this... sometimes when you power off and on too quickly, it just goes dead. It will not respond for a long time. Don't panic. Stop pushing the power button. Just unplug everything. The hard drive, the HDMI, the power, unplug everything. Go walk your dog, and when you come back, and connect everything again, it will power up. This happens to other Clearclick devices I have, so when it happened with this device, I didn't panic. I knew what was up.

* Power port is micro usb. Again, at $250, I'd like to see USB-C. Micro usb is antiquated, and their cords are prone to get damaged.

* You will need a HDMI splitter to bypass HDCP, as well as be able to turn off your Clearclick when you're not recording, and still watch TV. In my scenario... my source goes into my splitter, and my splitter has TWO outs. One goes into the Clearclick, and the other goes to my projector. This way, I can turn off my Clearclick if I'm not recording, and still watch my projector. If I connect the source directly to the Clearclick, and then go OUT from the Clearclick to my projector, then I would get their ugly icons on my projector. In my pictures, the source is my Nvidia Shield, you'll notice a row of white icons at the top. There is no option to hide these icons in passthrough mode. So if you use the Clearclick as a passthrough, you will get those ugly icons on your big screen. So even if you're recording sources that do not need a HDMI splitter. I'd still get one anyway because using the hdmi passthrough is not pretty. However, the good thing is that the files you record, will not have those icons.

In conclusion, if this weren't a Vine item, I would send it back. Having said all that, it's possible that my expectations may be unreasonable for a very niche product. If a big company like Sony or Samsung create a polished standalone capture device like this, maybe it'd be $500-$600. In which case, you'd be pretty happy with the ClearClick. If you learn to live with the quirks, it's a nifty piece of tech. Hopefully, they can improve on the user experience through firmware updates. I'll go 3-Stars this time.

title: Easy peasy back up!
text:
I read some of the reviews and concerns. Many are saying you need the original power adapter. My testing says that is NOT true. I plugged this cube into two separate charging hubs, not apple brand, and both scenarios worked.

You need a micro SD card (not included). Some of the questions in the Q&A shows that shoppers don't realize this. There is no built in hard drive in this cube, you provide the storage.

Turning off auto-sleep/auto-lock may get you through thousands of pictures in one shot. This is what I mean... I'm no stranger to trying out different back-up programs. The current program we use is from Plex. When the iphone is backing up to my plex server, the iphone doesn't know that plex is working, so it goes to sleep after about 50 pictures. When it goes to sleep, plex stops backing up. So I always turn off auto-sleep prior to backing up. With the Qubii, the iphone KNEW that it was working, so it "almost" never went to sleep. I said almost because after 4000 files, for some reason, the phone went to sleep. Still, this is much, much, better than the plex app. When I started Qubii again, it picked up where it left off and backed the remaining 1000+ files. But I did the test one more time to make sure! I cleared the micro sd card, and I reset the Qubii count. This time I turned off auto-sleep/auto-sleep on the iphone, and it backed-up the entire camera roll of over 5000 photos and videos in one shot! More trials need to be done to conclusively say this thing can't get through 5000 files without the auto-sleep disabled.

After backing up everything, you should remove your SD card from the Qubii and transfer them to a larger permanent hard drive where you store your collection. title: As advertised
text:
USB Type-C is just a super complicated situation all around. The ports themselves can be USB 2.0, 3.0, 3.1, 3.2, thunderbolt 3 or thunderbolt 4. I'm probably missing something there. That only covers data transfer speeds. For power, a Type-C port can be rated for multiple voltages and amperages. To protect the consumer from disaster (or they try anyway), each type-c product needs to be equipped with a chip that allows it to negotiate the speed and voltages. This includes the cables. The situation with cables is just as complicated. A cable may only be able to charge at 5v and not carry any data. They may carry only usb 2.0 data. Better ones may be rated for high speed data but not high wattage. Others have both high speeds and are rated for up to 100w. Good luck trying to find the right cable once all of them are dumped in a drawer somewhere.

This 240W USB C to USB C Cable 6.6ft is yet another odd one in the bunch. It is rated for high charging speeds but is only USB 2.0 for data. Why is it necessary though? I have a Dell Inspiron laptop that has a discreet NVidia RTX 3050 processor. This means that it has a high power demand.

This Dell was also designed to charge only from a USB type-c port and the input power must be 130w. So began my search for a charger that I can take with me when I'm away from my desk. I was able to find a macbook style charger that outputs 140w but I didn't own any cables that were rated for higher than 100w.

I came across this cable and connected everything up. During boot, the Dell's firmware still detected a low-powered charging device, but when I booted into Windows 11 and checked its power settings (after reconnecting the charger to the wall), Windows did not warn of an under powered charger as it normally would. I was then able to use this charging setup to play a graphics intensive game for over an hour with no sign of GPU or CPU throttling.

In the end, this cable allows me to have a portable solution for my laptop without having to lug around a standard laptop charger. It works.

title: Large 21" screen for better drawing experience
text:
I'm not a professional artist nor do I have a lot of experience with digital art, but that is one of the reasons that XP-Pen is a good choice for someone like me. Wacom rules the digital art world but for someone who is only a hobbyist when it comes to digital media, I have a hard time justifying paying the price that they charge. With that in mind, XP-Pen and Huion are the brands that I target for my budget.

Previously, I purchased a Huion Kamvas 13 and it was a great product but with my aging eyes, I needed a larger screen as even the 1080p resolution screen on that 13" screen was a little bit difficult for me to see without reading glasses. So when I had a chance to upgrade to a 21" XP-Pen, I took it.

This puts me in a situation where I am able to compare the two brands with each other. Both brands sport very similar pens and both screens have a matte surface to give the pens some friction for that "paper-like" feel. I'd say it's more like pen on paper feel, whereas I would've preferred to have more friction but it's something I think is worth training myself to get used to.

The XP-Pen drivers are on-par with the Huion drivers. Once the drivers are installed, it will show a preview of the screen layout that you have set up in Windows and it's quite easy to select the correct screen area that the pen should direct its touch to. From there, the pen buttons can be customized to macros that fit your needs and of course you can set up a different macro for each app that you use.

There are no additional macro assignable buttons on the XP-Pen screen, but there are standard OSD menu buttons at the top of the monitor, just like any other monitor you may own.

I'm happy to report that the XP-Pen drivers run alongside the Huion drivers without conflict. I have a Huion macro pad to make up for the buttons that are missing on the XP-Pen monitor.

So not being a professional artist, I do still try to spend as much time as I can to learn digital drawing and painting. In addition, I have interest in video and photo editing, so this pen tablet is great for selecting subjects using the rotoscope tool in video editor or smart select tools in image editors. Then there's 3D modeling. The pressure sensitive pen is great for sculpting in Blender and other 3D modeling programs. This is also something I'm trying to learn as well.

Despite the multitude of uses that I described above, I also don't have the desk space to devote to this 21" beast. It means that I needed a way to safely stow it. I didn't expect that I would find a carrying case for a large monitor, but to my surprise, that's exactly what I found! This [[ASIN:B099ZSDQ6V KISLANE travel carrying case]] fits the XP-Pen perfectly. It is big enough for the monitor, including its adjustable height stand and has plenty of pockets for the power adapter, pen, usb cables and my Huion macro pad. I didn't think there would be a market for people who thought "hey, it'd be great if I could bring my 24-inch iMac on my trip!", but thanks for that! Now I have a case for my 21" pen tablet.

One thing to note: I ran into an issue with inconsistent pressure with the XP-Pen drivers where I would run the pen across the scree and the darkness or width of the line would be very jittery. It was only alleviated by turning off the setting called Microsoft Ink. After my computer upgraded to Windows 11, I haven't seen this issue. So if it happens to you, try turning of that setting.

title: A good product that's getting better
text:
I've been obsessed with fully wireless earbuds for years and have tried out at least a dozen different ones throughout.

I fully support some in the $30 range, I had a pair of old soundcores that worked great. I've also tried the more expensive Samsung Galaxy Buds (2018 version), which worked well enough. I've also tried some mid-range ear buds in the $70 range. Earbuds have gone through some growing pains with drop off issues between the left and right buds and battery life. In my experience, I believe the $30 buds are great value and >$100 buds are worth it only if they have good sound and good app support. For me every one of the $70 buds that I have purchased have broken down in less than three months, so I'd say stay away from those.

Now on to the review:
The Cleer Audio, Ally Plus II True Wireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds are in the >$100 range (although just barely) but in the last few weeks that I've used them, I truly believe they are worth their asking price. I will of course update this review if they break down in a few months.

There are so many wireless earbuds being produced these days, which most imitating the airbuds with their ugly stalks in one form or another, Cleer has gone with a tear-drop shape and capacitive controls that I appreciate. I purchased the tan-colored buds and they don't stand out like a pair of white or black buds would. There is only a single dim light on the earbuds to indicate charging status and they are the in-ear-canal style of earbuds.

Features:
- Light-weight.
- Charging/carrying case supports type-c connection as well as wireless charging. Interoperable with products designed for airbuds wireless charging.
- Long battery life. I listen to audiobooks and they have lasted for hours while I worked on chores around the house.
- Passthrough with good app support (more on it later)
- Active Noise cancellation
- Can be used as a single earbud without having to pair each separately
- Touch controls: Only tap, double tap, and triple tap are supported. Configurable through the app.

The App:
When I first received the Cleer earbuds, the app was unimpressive. There was a single slide bar that changed the balance between noise cancellation and passthrough, a equalizer with no presets (and no reset for that matter), and there was limited control over what the tap functions did.

Since then, the app has been updated and the earbuds had a firmware upgrade. While the app still has room for more improvement, they did separate the passthrough, normal, and noise cancellation modes into separate controls. Passthrough now has a slider to control the strength of the surrounding noise and the noise cancelling has a "smart noise cancel" mode. In addition, a new personalized audio feature was added. The app takes you through a hearing test and adjusts the sound to your hearing levels. Quite cool.

The limited controls over the touch function is still there and the barely passable equalizer is still there but I'm hoping that they will be improved in future updates.

title: An excellent first generation product from Nikon
text:
Full disclosure: I'm a Sony E camera fan and use them for work, so giving this Nikon 5 stars means a LOT from me.
I was skeptical about Nikon's entry into the mirrorless camera world, since in the past they saved their higher end specs for DSLRs, and didn't take the mirrorless market seriously (*cough* Nikon 1 *cough*). However the full frame Z cameras got a lot of positive acclaim, and this Z50, their first APSC crop sized mirrorless, is a heck of a lot better than any first generation product has any business being!
First let's talk about ergonomics- the camera feels great, not point-and-shoot tiny in your hands. Definitely smaller and lighter than a DSLR, but more substantial than a phone, as a camera should be. It has a touch screen, which is AWESOME for touch-focus and really helps avoid the "how to I change that setting" learning curve- generally, just press on the icon and you can change the setting. Yet it doesn't RELY on the touch screen, there are plenty of physical buttons and dials, many of which are customizable and can be assigned to functions you need more often. Essentially, this is a camera that's got more than one way to do most things and therefore will adapt to YOUR workflow rather than force you to learn its own. The screen can also tilt up or down, and lets you flip it around on the bottom to see selfie-style if desired. This is one area that seems a little odd for me- other cameras like the Sony A5100 flip UPWARDS, so you can see over the camera if taking a self portrait. Or the Panasonic GH series articulates sideways. This, only flips DOWN. Which means if mounted to a tripod, you can't see the display at all. That is alright since honestly most of the higher end full frame cameras don't even let you flip the display around at all these days. The fact that you can, even if in a silly orientation, is better than nothing and a welcome feature.
Image quality seems pretty great, the kit lenses are adequate. I really liked the 50-250, as 16-50 with variable aperture feels very limited in creativity (however this lens is necessary as a "walkaround" standard zoom length). To be fair, I'm spoiled by my pro constant f-stop lenses that I use on my other cameras, so I'm rarely impressed by the performance of budget friendly kit options. I'll admit that for kit lenses these really perform remarkably well, but I'm hoping Nikon rolls out some awesome affordable Z-mount DX lenses soon. Cropping in to view pixels at 100% zoom size, the image holds up and seems reasonably sharp. Nikon colors are there as well, which are admittedly excellent. As with any new system, there aren't a lot of lenses available yet unless you adapt from other mounts. Nikon has F-mount adapters for native adaption, and I've read good things about third party adapters for other camera types as well (Canon, etc... I've even seen a Sony EF adapter for sale!). Sadly, I don't have access to any adapters at the moment, so I'm stuck judging imaging quality by the included kits for now.
Now for video, this gets even more interesting. Nikon has done a bang-up job supporting popular frame rates and resolutions (4k at 24p? Hello filmmakers!). In my tests, the quality of the video was very clean and sharp. I haven't noticed much in the way of moire or aliasing yet, and it has a clean HDMI out option as well if you want to record externally or view on a bigger monitor while filming. Unlike certain other cameras (like the Sony a6300), it is able to keep the rear display ON while also using the external monitor / recorder, and also recording internally at 4k. Other prosumer crop cameras have turned off the internal display when doing all of those things at once. It does support a microphone jack which means you can use this for recording interviews, however it is missing a headphone jack to monitor the audio levels. That's a huge omission if you wanted to use this as a semi-pro video making tool.
Thankfully, I found a workaround: If you get a cheap HDMI monitor (they have for around $100 that can attach to the hotshoe mount), they often have audio jacks. I happen to have a couple by Feelworld that do exactly that, and I was able to plug headphones in and hear the audio while in recording mode live. Well, semi-live at least. When recording 4k, there was a brief delay in the A/V playback, I'm guessing because the throughput required for 4K creates some latency. But the point is that you COULD hear it, and therefore make sure the volumes are appropriate and audible, and thereby making it possible to use the Z50 as a more pro level tool.
All in all, this is an excellent entry into the market by Nikon. Whether you are a beginner looking to eventually start using semi-pro tools or a seasoned pro looking for a budget friendly walkaround or B-cam, this is a very impressive value.

title: Great quality. Works with Canon 60D.
text:
[[VIDEOID:13857efa3820e6eb7b02a0a8943823dd]] I am reviewing the ‘AODELAN Camera Wirless Shutter Release Timer Intervalometer for Canon EOS 800D, 200D, 80D,750D, 650D, 600D,1300D, 1200D, 90D, M6 Mark II, 6D Mark II, 7D Mark II; Fujifilm X-T3; Olympus E-M1 Mark II‘

I have been looking for a wireless shutter release for my Canon 60D for quite some time now but haven’t been able to decide what kind to get. There are quite a few out there from basic to full featured like this one seems to be. Most of what I shoot is landscape or product photos but I would like to do more in the line of Time-Lapse, Wildlife and Night Photography. This Aodelan looks to have a bit of everything that I needed. So far I have only used it for product photography and I used it briefly with a Time-Lapse. During that little bit of testing I found that I could only set the remote to take a total of 199 images and set intervals. I set it for 199 shots at 10 second intervals but was cut short by rain hitting my gear and only ended up with 149 shots. (See attached video) There really should be a way to set it for much longer as 199 shots compiled into a Time-Lapse is only a few seconds long. I am still learning this device so hopefully I can figure out if 199 image is truly the limit. If so, this is very disappointing..

As for the Wireless Shutter remote, it functions perfectly for my needs. I am able to set the shot up and wirelessly trigger my shutter with the remote from quite a distance, which will be perfect for capturing the Hummingbirds that frequent my kitchen window feeder. I will be able to set up the shot outside and trigger the shutter from inside the house when the Hummingbirds are in position. Night photography will also be fun to try, as I can now remotely trigger the shutter using Bulb mode without causing any camera shake. You can also use this kit wired and only need to plug the Transmitter into the Remote port on the camera, but personally I will mainly be using this kit Wirelessly.

The quality and features of this kit are really nice. Both the Transmitter and Receiver are made of what seems to be a good quality plastic. Both devices take 2XAA batteries which were not included. Battery life seems to be good thus far and I would imagine that my newly installed batteries should last a good long time.

Though I am still learning this kit, I did notice that when trying to take continuous shots, it seems to limit the camera from shooting as fast as it is capable of. This isn’t a huge deal (because this isn’t what I plan to use this kit for) but I thought it worth mentioning.

Other than the 199 shot limit when shooting Time-Lapse I am very pleased with the overall performance and quality of this kit and think it is good value for the money.

*Update - I just found the setting that will allow unlimited shots during the "Timer" mode. This will allow you to take as many shots as desired for Time-Lapse photography. This is really nice though I do wish you could limit it to a higher number than 199. How about 999? lol

title: Nice sounding, versital studio mic - large and solidly constructed
text:
This is a USB based studio mic that's mounted on a desktop stand. The mic can be swiveled in the stand to tilt forward or back as needed. The mic itself is solidly constructed... it feels very well made. The stand is similarly constructed and should sit firmly in place. Theres a headphone volume control on the front of the body, along with a mute button, and similarly positioned on the rear of the body is a polar pattern selector switch and a gain control for adjusting the mic's recording output. The pickup patterns available are:stereo, omni, cardioid and figure 8.

I have some typical studio mice, but this is my first USB based mic, so I ran it through some typical trials to see how it fared. First of all, I found the sound to be accurate and with just the slightest "edge" - which seems to give it a slight touch of presence, especially in cardioid mode. Playing with tv he polar patterns, I could tell a bit of change in tone as I moved in close or away from the mic when in cardioid or figure 8 pattern - the effect is expected for these patterns and, though slight, were definitely there. Omni mode (picks up sound from all directions) did not show this effect (you would not expect it to). As for off axis rejection, I tried singing off to one side and then the other. Again, it performed as expected with no rejection whatsoever in omni mode. Rejection was minimal in cardiod and figure eight mode, though. (I would have preferred more). Also, in cardioid mode (signal is picked up directly in front of the mic only), I found the directional pattern a little wide. I like to use this mode specifically to isolate what's directly in front of the mic from the rest of the room. It works as it should, but I would have preferred it to be slightly more "directional". Finally, for stereo mode... this probably had the most impressive sound. It truly delivered a stereo sound... evenly balanced, with no dropout in the center. I even snapped my fingers on either side to see if it would pick up properly... it performed exactly as it should. As for sensitivity, it picked up the central heating unit fans in the background (just like a studio mic should), so some form of noise reduction would be called for (or turn off the hvac). Self noise did not appear to be evident - another specification that would have been nice for them to share (I dont even know if self noise is an issue with USB mics- this one didnt seem to have a problem with it).

Most people that I know would be interested in things like diaphragm size... that kind of detailed technical information is lacking from any of the paperwork that comes with this mic. It makes reference to a three capsule head, which makes me assume theres 3 diaphragms in there with the pickup pattern selector turning them on and off as needed, but no other info is provided.

All in all, I was impressed with this mic... it sounds good and has great versatility. It simply plugs into your computer's USB port and you're good to go (you may have to select the mic through your systems settings page). I think it would be ideal for any desk top application, podcasts, etc. It even has a screw in stand mount on the bottom. The only thing missing is some kind of a shock mount system, like a spider mount, or something), to shield it from noises that may vibrate through the desk to the mic. I suppose, sitting it on some foam would serve to isolate it.

title: That is utterly pathetic: I just benchmarked my 6+ year old Western ...
text:
Patriot: I am reaming your drive for one reason: it is supposed to be a premium drive, but it has utterly ABYSMAL small (e.g. 4K) random write speeds.

The benchmark below was done with CrystakDiskMark (all default settings) on your drive as shipped (bizarrely formatted as FAT32). Note the 4K write results of < 0.040 MB/s. Reformatting the drive as exFAT changed most of the results very little, except the sequential write dropped to 143 MB/s for some reason.

That is utterly pathetic: I just benchmarked my 6+ year old Western Digital SATA hard drive, and it gets ~1 MB/s for those same 4K random write speeds. Oh, and that hard drive is fully encrypted with TrueCrypt, which handicaps it even more...

Patriot: update this product NOW. Dump whatever craptastic flash controller you are using, and put in a real SSD controller. A premium drive needs uniform premium performance (as well as the best ECC).

And while you are at it, dump the el cheapo plastic housing and use a quality metal, like aluminum (both for the strength as well as the heat dissipation).

It saddens me to have to rate this drive so low, because it actually has a lot of potential. First, I like its size, which is small enough. Second, the slider mechanism actually seems robust. Normally I hate slider thumb drives because of bad experiences with Sandisk's awful sliders, which have broken multiple times on me. Third, the fact that this drive has OK sequential read and write performance means that you have solved half the performance problem.

I bought this drive on impulse late at night without spending sufficient time scouring reviews. I am adding this very negative review to ward off other potential buyers who also might need a drive that has decent 4K performance.

I so hope that someone comes out with a smallish enough thumb drive that consistently performs like a SSD. The closest drive that I know of is Visiontek's.

title: Endured the elements for four wintry months, and my headphones survived intact!
text:
I wanted a simple hardshell case to attach a carabiner to and sling my noise-canceling headphones off my backpack. This did the job. It was fine, I was pleased.

Then I came back from a December trip to Helsinki and somewhere between baggage claim at DFW and my front door, the case - with my beloved headphones, a battery bank, and my Apple rapid charge block - vanished.

I was heartbroken. I filed reports. I checked with my Lyft driver. I went through my backpack and suitcase over and over and over again. I poked the bushes around my apartment building. Nothing.

Fast forward four months to today. I took the trash out and as I came back up the stairs, I saw something dark colored under the feral cat shelter on my patio. In all these months I’d never noticed it. But when I lifted the shelter, there it was. Filthy, scratched up, covered in pollen - my headphone case. I believe I knocked it under there while I was looking for my house keys.

In the last four months the DFW area has seen torrential downpours, freezing sleet, and even snowdrifts. My porch often catches the brunt of these storms. And yet when I zipped the case open, my headphones and battery bank and charging block were perfectly fine. Not so much as a dust mote on them. Everything was still fully charged and absolutely totally functional. As if they hadn’t just spent four months outdoors in Texas’ wacky winter weather under a cat hutch. Completely perfect.

And the case may be fine externally as well once I take some Clorox wipes to it.

Anyway. Good case, STUPENDOUS dang value for the cost.

title: Leaps and bounds above the rest.
text:
Edit 11-20-2018

Mobile app iOS,

I noticed as some others have that I was unable to see a camera remotely yesterday. I had previously setup and tested the app with just 3 cameras. Nothing would bring the new cameras into view. Well almost nothing, I removed the app from the phone and reinstalled it, now all cameras are showing remotely.

Original :
I was a low voltage installer in years gone by and this brought back memories of why I no longer like crawling in attics at this age. Seriously though the unit is superb. Its not that bad of an install, its just me hating crawling in attics after having done it for so many years.

It came packaged really well. I was surprised at how well it was protected. We purchased the 16 channel NVR for future expandability. I put cameras all over the place. They are arranged to keep track of important areas as you would expect. The image is great. Better than I had hoped for.

The cables are not really internet ready, each cable only has 4 wires in it. I would rather have had a fully functional cable.
Upon taking the DVR out of the box, there was a small rattle inside, more of a piece of plastic moving around. Like a broken tab during assemble.

Installation activities.

The cables also a little short for larger homes, though they do sell longer versions. In most of my use cases the cables were fine. It's just 3 were all the way across the home in a far corner. I could have used another 10'.
So, I simple ran my own cable and terminated the ends. No big deal for me. However if you think you'll have enough and your getting close in your estimation, you better have one or two longer ones. The 60' cables seem to be a standard in the security camera kits.

The cable protector/environmental protection covers are a little large, not overly so. Just notating it here for others. You'll need to make sure you have extra room behind the camera. Most people will not see this issue. Make sure and use a drill bit big enough for the protector to pass though if it will be placed inside a wall, or overhang etc. You are not just drilling a hole for the cable. Look at the camera and you'll see the size you need to make it. I also ended up needing a longer HDMI cable, the one that came with this was about 6' I needed a 10' due to my particular situation. Not a mfg. fault, just my use case. So this one went into the spare bin and one in a 10/12' came out.

The first day, I needed to arrange things in my AV closet, and add a plugin. You may wish to have a licensed electrician preform this, if it's needed.

We started about 1 pm and finished about 7 putting in the NVR, 3 cameras, pulling 3 new wires, terminating those wires. The second day we started at 9 am and finished at 8 PM, with the remaining cameras. Though we had some extremely challenging placements this day. Your install time may or may not be this long, or it could possibly be longer.

Use :

As to the cameras they work really well, I was surprised at how well the picture looks and the microphone, well its as another user put it almost too good. You can go into settings and turn down the volume., Make sure you do that for cameras that are internal, aka in the house. If you using a monitor it may not be necessary that much. But ours is piped into the living room tv, and the kids or I, leave the volume up. You'll clearly know it when you switch over to the camera system and click on the camera.

Notes:

For anyone looking for answers here its also a good bet to look at the Swann forums. There are some good topics from other users there as well. Especially for users who may be asking more technical or unique issues. For anyone looking at this I would suggest also looking at some youtube videos there are a few that go over some of the options in the NVR settings. Like setting recording limits etc. Motion detection and so forth.

End results / Opinion:

I am more than pleased with my purchase, it far lives up to my desires. I wish I had bit the bullet and done this earlier on. Like years ago, but oh well its up now and I am more than happy. It's a little large purchase, money wise. But I personally think it was well worth the money at least for us.

This replaced a wireless competitor and its leaps and bounds above it.

title: Works well with a single computer but uncertain with a 2nd computer
text:
Update 1/22/23
I was able to resolve the HDMI to DisplayPort issue. The HDMI to DisplayPort adapter, along with the corresponding cables, weren't providing a sufficient signal to the KVM switch. I found an active HDMI to DisplayPort unidirectional cable with a USB-A power plug. I didn't have to use the USB-A portion of the cable. But switching to this unidirectional cable resolved my issue fully. I can now fully recommend this KVM switch. If any of you are experiencing an issue converting HDMI to DisplayPort, be sure to find a cable that states the specific signal flow from each end of the cable.

There's a lot to like with this KVM switch. It's compact, supports dual monitors, 4k @ 60Hz display and easy to switch between computers. However, I couldn't get the 2nd computer to display its output onto a single, external monitor.

Pluses
1. Small, compact, unobtrusive
2. Includes 4 DisplayPort cables and USB cables to hookup 2 separate computers
3. 4 USB ports to add keyboard, mouse, etc
4. No noticeable video degradation

Minuses
1. USB power adapter not included
2. Unable to get a 2nd computer to display its output onto a single monitor

I hooked up a Lenovo laptop to the 2nd computer USB port and single DisplayPort using an HDMI to DisplayPort adapter. I tried a few different options, but no matter what was tried, I couldn't get the laptop's output to display onto a single monitor. There was no issue hooking up the laptop's HDMI output directly to the monitor, so maybe the KVM switch just doesn't like the HDMI to DisplayPort adapter. I'm giving the device a 3 star rating because of it.

title: Charges!
text:
The Skyque USB Fitbit Flex Charger Cable works very much like the original charger that came with the Fitbit Flex. There is no difference in function or basic appearance; you plug the Flex tracker into it the same way, the cable is the same length, and it has no fewer or added features. It charges the Flex just as efficiently as the charger I received in the box with my Fitbit, although it charges very fast so a couple of minutes faster or slower would be hard to notice unless I were really timing it carefully, and I’ve also lost my original charger anyway.

Make SURE YOU ORDER THE RIGHT CHARGER FOR THE TYPE OF FITBIT YOU HAVE. They are not interchangeable. I know that’s very obvious, but still, just triple check before you pay for something you can’t use. It’s not Prime shipping so I don’t know what their return policy is.

This charger does not come with a reset button. I do have a second charger that replaced my original but that one also doesn’t have a reset button, and I never used it with the manufacturer’s charger (fortunately I never needed it). Apparently it is actually a pinhole (good thing so you don’t push it by accident), so it’s easy to miss noticing that you actually have it.

It is not clear by the product heading, but I think it is only the Fitbit Charge cable that is meant to have the “quite a longer length.” Either way the charger I received was identical to the other replacement charger I received from a different company, and apart from this lack of a reset pinhole that may or may not be on all OEM Fitbit charging cables it is also identical to that one in both length and otherwise.

I actually got the Skyque USB Fitbit Flex Charger Cable so that I would have a second charger for my Fitbit Flex, not to replace a lost or damaged one. I am actually on my second charger though, since I lost the original one, so this is not a scenario that is out of the question. I really like my Fitbit, but since it runs for about a week between charges I rarely think about charging it until it is pretty dead, and when I do charge it I forget to put it back on. For these reasons I thought getting a second charger to keep in my purse or in my car would be a good idea, because that way I could charge my Flex while I am driving if I forget to charge it at home (which has the added bonus of not risking leaving the Fitbit at home after I charge it).

There is nothing overly special about this charger, but there is also nothing bad to say about it; it does what it is supposed to do, is easy to use, and arrived quickly. If you need a replacement charger or extra travel charger for a Fitbit there is no reason not to consider a Skyque charger.
