title: Very nice little camera
text:
Quite impressive overall. It's SMALL yet I wish it was just a little bit smaller. I have yet to read the manual cover to cover but have enjoyed snapping pictures in the automatic and manual modes so far.

The size of the S410 was one of its two biggest selling points. I want a camera I will have with me, not one that's at home taking up space. The other thing I wanted was decent to good image quality, and what I've seen so far makes me think that this camera is a good choice.

I ordered a second battery and used an inverter I already owned to charge it in the car. Much cheaper than the Canon car charger. The manuals are (somewhat comically) also very small little books. A useful road-map poster of features is included along with a quick-start guide, which is always square one as far as I'm concerned.

Color reproduction seems very good. Clarity is decent at this point. I obviously need to read the manual to understand everything that's going on, and it's clear that there's a LOT of technology stuffed into this little gem. The controls are well-placed and the menus seem concise, operation overall is quite snappy. I'm pleased. The LCD screen is extraordinarily bright and crisp. Time between shots is acceptable, pretty quick, really, and time-to-first-shot is very good.

I don't think you'd need a case for the camera. Wrap it in a handkerchief if you're worried it will get scratched. I like the lens being covered by two little doors that close on power-off. Keeps the lens safe and you don't have a loose lens cap to worry about. The camera is smooth, no protrusions to catch on anything. It's a great looking little thing. It's a little bit heavier than you'd think it would be. I wish it was a little bit lighter and a little bit smaller. Which seems greedy given how light and small it is now!

One thing I like in particular is the B&W setting. Shooting in black and white is something a lot of folks who didn't spend time taking Intro to Professional Photo back in college may not have experienced, and it's worth checking out, particularly for portraits. Black and white can tell a better story than color.

I'm probably being unfair giving this camera only four stars -- there are certainly no glaring faults, far from it, but this was a realistic choice for me, a camera that I can take everywhere with me, and, no, for this price it's not going to perform like a Canon D20 which is ten times the price, but it is MUCH smaller and twice the resolution of my beloved old Nikon 950 (circa 1999). Maybe I'm expecting D20 performance at a S410 price..?

For its size and the price, this camera is quite a good value and is everything I expected, very well put-together and quick. A good choice. Not film-quality images, but very good for what it is. A good balance of resolution, size and weight. A handy, good quality camera to snap photos of the kids with, small enough to have with you everywhere you go. Not that I'd mind the "inconvenience" of having a Canon D20 over my shoulder 24/7... but that's simply not in the budget!

No regrets at all having chosen the S410!

Five years later: I had dropped my S410 and I couldn't use most of the functions, so I shipped it off to Canon to be repaired (for $100, ouch)... and it stopped working after about a month. I was sharply disappointed. I didn't want to send it off AGAIN (another $100), and I was unhappy having no camera. Canon offered a "loyalty program discount" or whatever they called it, I could buy a refurbished next-step-up camera from them for about $150, but after the $100 wasted on a not-very-robust repair I was reluctant to do that. I ended up buying a used S410 off a popular auction site. I expect things to last basically forever, so I was disappointed that I was clumsy enough to drop my camera and disappointed again that Canon's repair was extremely short-lived.

title: Securely holds the Blink camera
text:
When I installed my Blink XT2, I found I needed to move it a little lower so I could maybe see the face of the delivery person. Thinking I could unscrew the mount without removing the camera, I turned the camera to one side so I could access the screws. The camera fell to the floor. A little bit of friction is not sufficient to hold these cameras. That is when I started looking at these mounts which SHOULD be included in the box.

This is in several parts. Plastic camera-enclosing parts are held together with 4 small screws. The metal part is attached to the wall with 3 flat-head #6 screws.

Unscrew the adjusting part so the base of the mount can be attached to the wall. Do not try to adjust the angle unless this part is loose. Use care when tightening the screws - do it manually so the screws are not over-tightened. The aluminum base could be cracked by over-tightening.

The small screws that are used to attach the back cover to the front should be machine screws, and the posts into which they are screwed should be metal. This is my opinion and is because these screws will have to be removed and reinstalled every time the batteries are replaced.

One piece of plastic had a small 'tab' on it that had to be cut off before the back cover would attach to the front.

A hole in the bottom of the plastic is there to allow a charging cable to be attached. If you do not plan to use rechargeable batteries and have no need for the USB cable, plug the hole so insects do not go inside looking for a new home. I used a small piece of closed cell foam packing material (photo).

If you want to use these mounts with the earlier Blink cameras, you might want to use some foam so the camera does not move around inside the enclosure (photo).

I've been testing this Epson ProSense watch for the past week. I also have a 2-year-old Garmin Vivoactive HR watch that has most of the same features, but costs half as much. To the compare the two, I've been wearing one watch on each wrist and going on runs and bike rides to see how their readings compare. Both watches have daily step counters that give similar results (today, Garmin says 12044 steps while Epson says 12790 steps). 5% difference is close enough for me.

I know Garmin has a barometric altimeter, while Epson is using GPS elevation, which is notoriously inaccurate. Does Epson's terrible elevation data cause a wildly inaccurate calorie count? I could not find any information on Epson's calorie calculation in their documentation, so I really cannot trust it.

Both devices give me heart rate readings with graphs by time or broken out by training zones. The numbers look close enough for my purposes. Both devices also give me maps of my route, which is is nice to have for reviewing later, especially if it is a new route to me.

The Epson is a much larger device (both width and thickness), as shown in the photo. While the Garmin is not especially attractive, at least it is relatively unobtrusive. Epson is big enough to feel clunky on my wrist, especially if I am wearing it all day (to take advantage of the step counter).

Both devices have a smartphone app that syncs your data and also sends notifications to the watch. I'm using this watch with a Google Pixel Android phone. The Garmin app by default uploads your data to the Garmin website. With Epson, you have to upload to a 3rd party website like Strava, which may not be compatible with all the data that your device is collecting.

Notifications work much better with Garmin than Epson. For incoming phone calls, both Garmin and Epson will display the caller ID or contact name so I don't have to pull out my phone to see who is calling. For incoming emails, Garmin displays the sender name and subject line, while Epson just says "you have mail". For text messages, Garmin shows the contact name and message. Epson shows no notification for text messages.

The only advantage (for my use case) that I can find with this Epson watch is the much longer battery life. Garmin claims 1 week of battery life with the GPS off or 13 hours with the GPS on. Epson claims 46 hours of battery life with the GPS on, which I suppose is great for some ultra endurance sports. For me, I never exercise more than 8 hours in a day.

title: Received a used drive. At first Amazon refused a refund.
text:
I was immediately suspicious of the box when I saw it.

It looked like the security tape had been lifted and then reapplied as can be seen in the photo I included with this review.

This was an item sold and shipped by Amazon.

I went online to watch unboxing videos of the same product so that I might be able to spot signs of a fake product when I opened it.

I called Amazon and verified that I could return the product for a refund even if opened and then took an unboxing video of it while on the phone with an Amazon rep.

I couldn't tell from looking at the drive or the rest of the packaging that anything was wrong with it.

I told the Amazon rep that I would check with Samsung the next next day to see if they could verify if it as an authentic Samsung serial number and as a new product.

I expressed my concern that even if it was a Samsung product that it might be used and I would never have any way of knowing. Or even if I could tell it was used after I installed it I would then be in the position of having to uninstall the drive in order to return it.

The Amazon rep told me that if anything was wrong with the product that Amazon would issue a refund without requiring me to return it if it was already installed in my computer.

Samsung verified the serial number the next day as being authentic and said that I could even tell if it had been used before as well by using their magician software program.

I thought the only way I would be able to detect if it was used was if there was old data on it left by someone else but Samsung said their software could detect if the drive had been written on before.

The catch is that that software can only be used to diagnose a drive after it has been installed internally to a direct SATA connection. Their software couldn't diagnose the drive through an HDMI connection to an external dock unfortunately.

Based on it having an authentic Samsung serial number, the assurance by Samsung that their software could detect both fake and used products and the assurance by the Amazon rep that I could receive a return-less refund if needed I went ahead and had the drive installed.

I figured the worst case scenario would be that it was a fake and/or non functional drive and I would have to take it out again immediately, the best case scenario was that it was a new and working Samsung drive and the in between scenario would be an authentic but used Samsung drive.

It turned out to be a used drive. It had been wiped and reformatted but it had been written to before.

I called Amazon back and told them the drive was verified as used and I expected a refund. At first the rep refused any refund and then said I would only receive a refund if I uninstalled the drive and sent it back.

I told them that was fine with me if they were willing to pay for both the installation and the uninstallation fees charged by a computer repair shop.

The Amazon rep of course refused either option so I directed him to get a suprivisor on the call and then played the recording of the conversation I had with the Amazon rep the day before....I got my refund immediately.

The big lesson here is to record the unboxing of any expensive items you buy, especially if the packaging looks tampered with or damaged.

Another lesson is to record your phone calls with Amazon reps or with any customer service person if you are calling up with an issue.

I learned a few things about this product and Amazon throughout this process.

These QVO Samsung drives store four bits of info per solid state cell. Most consumer SSD drives store only three and some expensive special purpose ones store just one.

These drives have a shorter life spans than three bits per cell drives and handle having large amounts of data written to them at slower speeds than three bits per cell drives. They should be cheaper as a result but often aren't.

Amazon has no way of tracking where a product comes from even if it was sold and shipped by them.

Amazon just puts all the Samsung 1TB 870 QVO drives into a bin regardless of whether or not Amazon bought them from Samsung directly themselves or they were supplied to Amazon by a third party seller.

Unless its an Amazon branded product that no one sells on Amazon but Amazon (Amazon basics, 365 Foods, etc) they have no way of knowing where it originally came from even if it is “sold and shipped by Amazon”.

Buyer beware.

title: Do Not Buy This Product--Manufacturer's Site Downloads Trojans And Malware--Lousy Docs/Support
text:
THIS REVIEW IS FOR THE ZBOX Bi323-U.

DO NOT BUY FROM THIS MANUFACTURER--REASONS:
The ZOTAC WEBSITE happily shows you the line of products available and that's were things stop being great. WHEN YOU ACCESS THE WEBSITE AND CLICK SUPPORT, DOWNLOADS (updated drivers, and so forth) OR OTHER LINKS YOU MUST CANNOT GET IN UNTIL YOU SIGN UP AND SUPPLY SOME PERSONAL INFORMATION, SUCH AS YOUR NAME AND EMAIL ADDRESS. When I was in the middle of installing the software, I needed updated drivers from Zotac and ran into this. I don't know about you, but I don't want to have to give up personal information to get what I need for a product I bought unless I wish to do that, and in this case the OS installation was being problematic so I really don't what to have to register a purchase for an item I may have to return or exchange.

TROJANS-MALWARE-AND VIRUSES ARE INCLUDED WITH DRIVER DOWNLOADS FROM ZOTAC'S website. Once I got in, and was able to download updated drivers, I unzipped the file. My VIRUS PROTECTION WENT NUTS over THREE TROJANS THAT RODE ALONG WITH THE ZIP FILE. I've included a screen shot of this for the review. Worst of all, the download could not be done on the ZOTAC unit because the install wasn't complete. I downloaded on another Windows 7 PC and after my virus software got rid of the infection in the zip file, I had to run a full scan of that PC using the virus app, as well as two others to make sure that PC was clean. Who needs this kind of nonsense from a seller/manufacturer's web site.

GOOD STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX Bi323-U
--It's a decent piece of gear... at least for now. I'll be back if it fouls up later on. The memory and hard drive installation couldn't be easier.
--Once you install an OS, it boots into the software very quickly.
--Windows 7, 8.x and so on install well.
--Debian 8.4.x installs on this unit as well. It takes some tinkering and it finally installs.
--I installed Win 7 Pro, and then removed it and installed Debian. Just wanted to see how easy it is to do that. Notes about Debian are at the end.
--For a very low end item, this isn't a bad choice so long as you're willing to set aside a few hours to set it up and are willing to put up with a poorly designed manufacturer/seller website, and poor customer service.
--For my purposes it was an okay choice. I had a few extra SSDs around as well as memory that were compatible with this unit, so this was a cheap solution to add an extra computer.

NOT SO GREAT STUFF ABOUT THE ZBOX-Bi323-U
--BE SURE TO SCAN EVERYTHING FROM THE ZOTAC SITE AND THE CD/DVD THAT COMES WITH THE UNIT
--The documentation is really thin, almost useless.
--At first boot, the BIOS screen appears and you may (likely will) have to change some settings. It's best if you're familiar with what the settings do and what they effect. TIP: the Legacy Boot seems the most reliable. Complete the settings, save and exit.
--The BIOS (after adjusting settings) looks for an OS on the hard drive or CD/DVD. It does not look at USB thumb drives or SD cards. Have the external CD/DVD attached with install disc inserted.
--How to get back to the BIOS or BOOT SEQUENCE settings DOES NOT appear on any boot screens after the first power on, as it does with most other systems. How to access the BIOS settings IS NOT included in the docs. You have to press F8 for the bios or Delete for boot sequence settings. Found it on the web.
--Zotac site uses a squeeze page to get your info before you can access anything useful.
--The combination SD reader/USB port is just weird. You cannot use this port for both at once.

About Linux (Debian 8.4.x)
--I installed this successfully after several attempts. Zotac's site shows Linux drivers, but they download only the Win 7 drivers. You don't really need them for a Linux install. Set the bios for Legacy Boot or it won't boot into Linux after an install. ISO DVD 1 is the only file you need for the install. Graphical install is the only option that worked out.
--DO NOT TRY AND CONNECT WITH DEBIAN MIRRORS FOR NEWER APPS, it fails on all. Later use terminal to upgrade.
--After a successful install, the Zotac restarts and you end up at the Debian login screen for you user id and password. The password is rejected. --Power off with the power button. Power back on and this time you can login with the credentials supplied at install.
AFTER LOGGING IN, your user ID won't be in SUDOERS. Use terminal, SU into root. After that, use apt-get update followed by apt-get upgrade.

2. I'd tell you the driver version that I downloaded 3/16/2018, but the Huion website has not added the link to this tablet driver in its regular listing of product drivers so I can't find it again. They need to fix this for a better user experience for those who do not have DVD drives so have to download the driver, or who want to easily check for driver updates.

3. As others have said, the two-finger up/down scrolling on the trackpad majorly sucks. If I take the sensitivity all the way up to the top, it will scroll three or four lines at a time, but if it's at a sensitivity that allows for varying brush strokes, it scrolls one line at a time. I was trying to set up Express Keys to scroll a page up or down at a time (accessed with the fn key on my Macbook Pro) to compensate for this, but the fn key is not included in the setup for keyboard shortcuts. For now, I'm using space and Shift-space on my laptop keyboard to scroll up and down in those programs (like Gmail) that won't respond to click/dragging the scroll bar with the stylus. Click/dragging to scroll with the stylus works well in some programs. I don't want to waste two Express Keys for something one ought to be able to do with trackpad gestures.

4. The pen nib works as a left click in some programs if held down, but not all of them, so I had to sacrifice my lower stylus button to be a left click; the upper stylus button is a right click, and that seems to be the very best use of that button for me. I wanted to put Cmd+S (save) on the lower button so if I hit the button by mistake it would do something useful, but I guess I'll just start getting used to that button as a fall-back when a pen-nib left click does not work. I do very much like the feel of this stylus.

I really like having the top row of the Express Keys set up like this:

UL: Cmd+- (zoom out) (default)
UM: Cmd+0 (fit to screen)
UR: Cmd++ (zoom in) (default)

The bottom row I'm going to live with for a while to see if I like it or need something else. I mainly do photocompositing sorts of work, so the left and right buttons are often-used commands, but they are also easily accessible from the keyboard without having to put the stylus down:

BL: Cmd+Z (undo)
BM: Cmd+S (save)
BR: Cmd+J (copy layer)

The BM key is the least useful for me because it's so easy to just hit Cmd+S on the keyboard to the left of the tablet. A special request, if even doable, for a future driver update would be to give us the ability to combine Shift, Control, Option, and Command keys from the keyboard with the express keys, which would extend the flexibility of the tablet's Express Keys mightily.

Now, this seems a natural for combining with Affinity Designer's one-letter shortcut keys, so now I'm going to make the time to learn them all. I have not tested how the brushes work yet because I don't do a lot with brushes, but layer-level work seems to be handling super-well. I've also done a bit in ON1 Photo RAW 2018, and so far, so good.

In short: I think this G10T is a fantastic product that, because it's just been released, will need some driver tweaking until it can be the mouse/MacBook Pro trackpad replacement I really want to get used to using all the time. Super build quality, super easy/clean to use, but iffy in the trackpad department.

title: Close to being a really nice player; needs some firmware tweaks
text:
This MP3 player, which I was given at a discount in exchange for my honest review, is sleek and lightweight yet potentially—via a firmware upgrade that I hope Lonve will consider—very powerful. (See my photo of the player lying on top of my MacBook Pro trackpad to get an idea of its size.) It can be listened to without hooking it up to anything else, either with wired headphones or through the surprisingly good-sounding on-board speakers. The view screen when the player is powered on is quite readable, and I love how the surface of the screen becomes a classy grey-bronze mirrored surface that is so clear you can use it to check your appearance. The ability to add up to a 32GB SDHC card you've preloaded with music or video is a great feature.

The included wired headphones are better than some I've listened to, although I prefer another pair that fits my tiny ears better; unfortunately, those are Bluetooth, so they won't work with this player. I will likely listen to the player my itself, with no headphones, through its speakers.

I can't five-star love this player because I can't set the time to a 12-hour clock and it doesn't allow for adding playlists, which I was thinking it did. Maybe I'm missing something, but I can't even start an album folder playing by tediously navigating to it in the Explorer; it appears you have to navigate all the way into the files in the folder and then start it playing, although I haven't even been able to get this to work. It takes too many steps and is so very aggravating that I usually just quit trying to play either music or video.

What really shines on this player is the radio. I'm sure reception will vary depending on where you are, but in Lexington, KY, I can pull in NPR very clearly and easily. It would be nice to be able to store favorite radio stations—if there's a way, I haven't figured it out after days of fiddling with the player—but I'm happy that I can leave it sets to my main station and it always comes back there even after I've powered off and then back on. If you're a person who likes to listen to the radio at night with the lights off, going to sleep, but don't like fooling with headphones, this will be a great little player for you.

The Game feature has a neat little Tetris-style game that's amusing while stuck waiting somewhere. The Photo feature is nothing to write home about, but it can be used to show off a few photos of your pets or kids or maybe a logo or graphically produced emergency contact info. There is an Autoplay Time setting you can set in the Settings/Photo. The text feature allows for reading text files, so you can take along a grocery list or study notes. I started to knock off an extra star (down to three) because of something I really dislike about this player, and that is the dedicated left-side button (one of only three) that seems to serve no purpose but to turn on the voice recorder. When I press it by mistake or forget that the On/Off button is the button on the right, not the left, the Recorder comes on. Then I get a file format error when I try to get out of it. It would have been better, I think, had they used that button for something more likely to be used constantly (Explorer with the ability to set either the internal C: card or the external D: card as the default for the button maybe) or, better, allow the user to define the function of that button via a Settings selection. I want to be able to disable the Recorder completely, although I know some people will want to have a recorder. But I hate it.

You do have the option of upgrading the firmware, but the instructions are very poor. When I select Upgrade in Settings/System (which you reach by scrolling down to the end, near the Language setting), I am warned to connect to USB. When I connect the USB cable to my computer, however, I get the Connect screen on the player and there does not seem to be any way then to access the System/Upgrade selection. The instructions, such as they are, are clear in how to navigate through the features and which of the two non-Recorder buttons (middle, right) to push in connection with the up/down, left/right arrows. But, needless to say, there are bugs in the player I am reviewing. Lonve has been good about getting back quickly with answers to questions, though, so I'm hopeful they'll work hard to get this one right.

title: Large, Unpowered, Professional Interface with quirks
text:
In my opinion, this unit makes the GH4 into a professional video camera. However, it's certainly not perfect. I begged the Nikon guy at NAB 2013 to build something like this for the D800, but nothing yet. Panasonic is listening. I'm commenting here because as of June 4, 2014, you cannot download the YAGH manual from Panasonic's website for details you may need.

1. Cost

It's more than the camera body, which is to say, really expensive. I can only hope the YAGH will fit future GH5 and GH6 camera bodies. Please, Panasonic: don't obsolete this thing.

2. Power

There is no internal battery. It has to have external power, supplied via the industry-standard 4-pin XLR. This is good and bad. Stated power requirement on the bottom plate is 12VDC at 1.4 amps.

Power is applied to Pin 4, Ground to Pin 1. (Pins 2 and 3 are not used.) The manual says voltage can vary from 11VDC to 17VDC. This means any professional AC camera supply or brick battery like an Anton Bauer 14.4VDC. (I'm using a 12VDC battery pack built from ten NiMH D-cells and supplies 10,000 mAhs.) You'll need a 4-pin extension power cord and drag the power supply with you. Hello battery belt? Sort of going backward. It would be great to have the ability to add lith-ion batteries somehow but perhaps it draws too much power for smaller cells.

The external power powers both YAGH and the GH4 body.

Once the YAGH is attached to the camera, an "Interface Unit" menu appears on the "Motion Picture" tab. There are many options. One setting allows you to set low battery warnings at 11, 12.5, 13.5 and 15 volts. This is very professional.

UPDATE Sept 26,2014: I built a 12VDC power supply from a computer monitor power supply and a 4-pin female XLR jack. I also have a 14.4 volt battery power supply. I found that if I leave the battery warning set to 13.5 for the one power supply the 12VDC power supply won't work. The battery warning settings actually stop the camera from working. Be sure to set the battery warning levels to match the batteries you are using.

3. Fan

Yes, it has a fan. You can barely hear it (can't hear it six inches away), but hot air blows out the left side when it's plugged in. I assume there's a lot of electronics inside to supply all the outputs. Have not demonstrated the fan can be heard by the camera-body's built in stereo mics.

4. Inputs:

a. the 4-pin XLR power plug

b. two, 3-pin XLR audio inputs, switchable between Line (0dB), Mic (-50dB) and 48VDC phantom power. A stereo/mono switch sends the signal from a single mic to both left and right channels. You can select which mics to use: the built-in stereo camera mics or the XLR inputs.

c. time code-in on one of the BNC connectors

d. the micro-HDMI plug that transfers the HDMI camera output signal to a full-sized HDMI on the YAGH unit. This HDMI interface is implemented clumsily; I hope there is a better reason than engineering laziness. It's basically a short Micro-to-Full HDMI extension cord. The dovetailed arm that sticks up on the unit holds the micro-HDMI cord with a plug. You mount the camera to the unit, open the rubber door on the camera's left side so that it sticks straight out of the camera, then slide the YAGH's dovetailed micro-HDMI plug into the camera, then tighten the tiny thumbscrew. The rubber door disappears into the dovetail arm and is not removed or abused by being bent back too far. This sturdy plastic arm with its metal dovetailed very definitely protects the extremely fragile Micro-HDMI socket on the camera body. (I personally would not directly connect a cable into the camera. One yank and your camera is broken. I thought the Mini-HDMI plugs on Canon 5D's and Nikon D800's were bad. This Micro-HDMI is even smaller and weaker. The YAGH solves the problem.) It would have been better if Panasonic had routed the signal through the bottom of the camera, but that would mean another 15 pins down there, and it's already crowded.

e. One drawback of this HDMI interface method: if you screw the dovetail in, it takes up the whole left side of the camera and you cannot pivot the flip-out viewfinder down at all and upwards only about 5 degrees. The whole point of the pivoting viewfinder is the ability to frame low- or high-angle shots. If you don't need to remote the HDMI to the YAGH (say you're using the audio interface and DC in and not monitoring via the HDMI) you can let the dovetail hang there, flopping in the wind, and allow the viewfinder to rotate.

5. Outputs

a. full-sized HDMI socket under a rubber door on the left side outputs 4:2:2 8bit or 4:2:2 10bit. You can't record both internally and externally if in 10bit. You access this setting while in "Creative Video Mode." The 8bit is good for sending to an external monitor while recording to the card.

b. 4, SDI BNC connectors under a rubber door on the right side, marked 1, 2, 3 and 4. They output different signals based on the resolution of the recorded signal.
- any of the four BNCs can output a 1.5G HDSDI signal if resolution is set up to 1080-29.97p.
- 3G-SDI is output on BNCs 1 and 2 if you record in 1080-59.94p or 1080-50p
- 1.5G-SDI Square Division (whatever that is) is output on all four BNCs as a group if you want to output the Cinema C4K (4096x2160-24.00p) or Broadcast 4K (3840x2160-24.00p/23.98p/29.97p). Apparently you will need all four BNCs to get enough bandwidth to send the 4K signals to an external monitor or recorder.

UPDATE: the four BNC SDI outs supply "QuadHD" -- that is, each delivers one fourth of a 3840x2160 picture or, four 1920x1080 streams. If you have a device that can accept QuadHD, you're in business.

6. Plug and socket covers

Minor point, but of some concern. The camera is not waterproof but is touted as "splash proof." To achieve this, rubber doors seal the camera all over. The bottom of the camera has two rubber seals that cover two sets of contacts -- one with five, one with 18 contacts. The YAGH unit has quite exposed corresponding spring-loaded pins sticking up. When you attach the camera to the YAGH, you obviously need to remove the four covers. There's no place to store them. You will want them if you split the units apart, especially the camera seals.

7. Audio Controls

a. two 8-segment LEDs indicating level: 4 green, 3 yellow, 1 red.

b. two approx. 1/2" diameter knobs to adjust level, shielded by a clear cover so they won't get hit accidentally yet are easy enough to adjust during a take without shaking the camera or making noise

c. brightness is adjustable to either "Hi" or "Low" via the Interface Unit menu item under the Motion Picture tab

8. Mechanical

a. two locating pins register to the camera body and are held tightly via the 1/4-20 tripod socket. It really becomes a single unit

b. Both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 threaded tripod mounts on the bottom. There's also a hole for the tripod plates that have an anti-rotation pin. Having both 3/8-16 and 1/4-20 allows you to use two screws to mount the YAGH to your tripod plate so it cannot rotate.

c. two 1/4-20 threaded holes are supplied on the lower front of the YAGH to allow mounting a set of matte box rods, once some third party supplier starts making the rod/rail adapter. The two holes are exactly 32mm apart and centered 85mm below the optical center of the lens, conforming to the 15mm Light Weight Support (LWS) standard.

d. It's still not too giant for hand holding, but it's getting there. It's really designed to be tripod mounted.

e. Because the YAGH extends forward of the camera and slopes downward, if you use one, the Metabones Speed Booster tripod foot must be removed for the adapter to fit the camera while attached to the YAGH. Fortunately, Metabones allows this and supplies necessary Allen wrenches and caps.

Overall, the YAGH is useful -- allows (well, requires) external power for long runtimes, protects the camera from HDMI socket damage, outputs all kinds of signals up to true 4K via SDI, allows timecode input and allows professional audio inputs.

However, if you don't need external power, SDI-out or HDMI-out, a simple audio interface like the JuicedLink Riggy [[ASIN:B009YLRZFE JuicedLink RM222 Riggy-Micro Dual-XLR Preamplifier with Phantom Power]] or a Beachtek [[ASIN:B009R89SNQ BeachTek DXA-SLR MINI PRO HDSLR Audio Adapter]] might suffice to get pro audio in.

text:

In general I prefer low lighting and have sensitive eyes and get migraines, and the low setting is pleasant, the higher settings are fine unless you're in the pitch dark and then It's too bright for me. The keyboard has all the functions and options like print screen and page up and down and mute/volume controls that I need. I haven't used all of them yet.

The palm/wrist rest is not padded but is comfortable and does have a "soft" feeling coating. It does has sturdy fold out upper feet.

The cord is approximately 71 inches (180 cm).

This is a very slim and comfortable low-profile keyboard that is full size and has great back-lighting options. If it came in multicolor backlighting for a similar price I would've purchased that one as well.

I bought this for a new Lenovo Y910 AIO Win 10 which hasn't arrived yet (thanks UPS for making me wait 3 MORE days now when I paid for 2 day prime shipping), but I tested it on my MSI GE70 laptop running WIn 7 Pro and it was literally plug and play, worked instantly.

The bottom row of keys (ctrl, windows, alt, spacebar, fn, ctrl, are much taller/raised which is a little weird at first (arrow keys and number pad keys match the rest of the low profile keyboard). I may just be noticing it because I have damaged extensor tendons in my dominant left hand which limits how high I can lift 3 of my fingers. Time will tell if I get used to it and stop noticing it.

I've uploaded many photos, one is a composite showing all lighting settings. The differences are much more apparent in person than I could capture on camera.

title: GREAT VALUE and GREAT SOUND
text:
I needed this receiver asap to replace a damaged one. I bought this outside of Amazon last minute, but 90% of my items I buy are from here and wanted to share my review. Took and image of the box, unit as well as remote. Also tested IMAX ENHANCED content.

I purchased this mid range one (TXNR797), instead of the higher end one was due to my set up. My old Onkyo was an introductory model that was 75 watts x 5.2.2 bought at the end of 2016 (5 speakers, 2 Dolby upwards firing speaker for Atmos and 2 sub-woofer outputs the .2) Upgraded to this receiver which is a 9.2 receiver that is 100x the channel, with THX mode for gaming, movie etc but also has more power and more room layout variation giving me room to add on and alter or audio in other rooms.

My home layout is 5.1.2 but I plan on adding 2 extra Dolby upward firing speakers behind making it a 5.1.4.

NOW THE REVIEW:

100 x the channel (each speaker), more than enough. My previous Onkyo I bought was a basic model that had Atmos and sounded great, but after I year I decided to go at least 100 per channel. With this one, due having more power at higher volumes, it sounds extremely clean and distortion free. I primarily use this for gaming on PS4 and movies (disk) in 4k/Atmos sound etc I do stream Hulu/Amazon etc but sound quality in those tend to be compressed and even they sounded decent.

For gamers, they do have a dedicated equalizer for action, RPG, stadium etc and various movie tweeks like THX gaming, THX film and THX music. Main reason I upgraded besides power is that THX sound does sound different, they also have tiny tweeks like 're equalizer' for content, removing harshness in sound. If you use THX mode, it will use a layout of 5.1, no matter what. Mostly due the contend being encoded in 5.1 originally. The only time it uses an up-converter to simulate the upwards/ceiling speakers is sound settings like 'Dolby Surround, DTS NEURAL X or any of the game tweeks'. If the content is DTSX/Atmos sound found in some blurays and all 4k films. Which are encoded for all films it will say DTS X or Atmos the same goes for IMAX ENHANCED films. Meaning its not simulated but encoded and yes they sound 50% better. The up converter still does give old and new films an extra layer of sound. Even went back revisiting films.

Imax Enhanced is only in some films streams and as of now, 4 or 5 films. The disk version tend to be more documentaries about the planet, south America, space etc at least for now. Audio was very clear. Now I just wish more films had Imax enhanced sound.

If you're watching something in any surround mode that is being delivered in 5.1 and up. You have the ability to target voice dialog. On the remote, click tone: which highlights bass, vocal and treble. When the receiver shows vocal hit + or - on the remote. What this does, it targets voice. Say for example, you can increase the main volume on the receiver to your personal liking but sometimes voice dialog varies per film and sounds lower. Instead of cranking up the main volume raising all speakers or increasing just the center speaker you can increase vocal by itself without pushing more power. You basically keep your own personal volume setting and just target voice. Max is 5 but never found myself going pass 1 or 2. To me, this is a major improvement I no longer have to fiddle with the unit and power anymore.

Overall, the unit is built solid, looks minimalist, has more than enough power for my middle to large living room. Has 2 sub-woofer outputs and can be used multi room for sound and chromecast and airplay ready. Its a basic streamer for audio from phone to unit and has audio apps built in like Spotify, Pandora etc it also has a wireless section to add Sonos wireless speakers. Since I use my PS4 Spotify app I do not use the built in functions. (I like to see artist info, lyrics ect on my tv) but sound quality was good when I tried it. If you dont use the tvs app for audio or game system you can use your phone to switch tracks and play music.

AUTOSETUP:

Onkyo did upgrade their auto setup to AccuEQ advanced and its much better. They removed standing bass waves while adding their own build in equalizing. They separated their equalizer tweek from stand waves. So you can now disable the Onkyo tweek but enable EQ only standing waves. AccuEQ did improve massively from the older version. If you lack bass, on a powered subwoofer check to see if receiver changed cross overs to low. The normal settings should be 80hz and sub at 120. This feeds the sub more bass. Only time they should be is if you have major massive speakers with built in woofers or powered subs inside. Even than most set them to 80hz. This is a good starting point and tweek from there. Mine get dropped to 40hz but id rather the sub to its job.

IMPORTANT:

Before messing with the unit, log into your Wifi, download the new firmware and than do the auto set up process.

TIPS: you can use the quick settings on the remote instead of pulling up the main receiver menu to turn on or off AccuEQ as well as other basic tweeks. See what sounds best for you. Some leave it on others don't and do their own tweeks.

Unit has updated to Imax enhanced sound option on Sep when I bought this 2019. It also updated the HDMIs to version HDCP 2.3, and can pass DOLBY VISION to a capable tv, just make sure you have a DOLBY VISION 4K PLAYER.

EDIT: 10/20/2019

Imax Enhanced content can be auto applied using the upconverter built in. Go to DTS/Imax section and select auto or on. I set mine to manual and select option on for bass feeding. The only requirement is have the audio streaming be DTS.

title: *almost* acceptable tablet priced competitively - charger warning
text:
Updated review at I'm guessing two weeks - OK, something to really be aware of here is this does not work with a significant amount of USB chargers I own. I was about to RMA the thing but decided to try it on the least used charger I had just for kicks.

You'll note the warning in the product description of "I can't charge the tablet" - you will find this quickly. See, USB you hear and think "universal" and no... this absolutely refuses to charge on any GaN charger I have (I have 3,) and a couple of wall chargers.. not working on a PD3 and I think a QQC3.1. I finally found the original charger and one no-frills charger that's part of my power strip would charge it. This isn't good.

I've only run into toys that had problems with chargers like this one did.

Additional to the review below - the battery life on standby is a lot better than expected. Had it not been alive after sitting unused for a week (just life, nothing about it,) I would have believed the unit had died.

Original review follows

This is an early review from someone who's worked with literally hundreds of Android devices as part of his employment for the past decade. This tablet has gotten use, but not been ridden hard and put up wet yet.

I did not have a lot of hope for performance when I got this. I needed an e-reader and general purpose tablet to supplement a S6 Lite I had working. I'm a little surprised at how well this did.

OK, first off while it "feels" faster than my much pricier S6 I hate "feels" so I ran Geekbench on the big name brand that's about 30% more expensive generally, and the Plimpton P6. Name brand comes in at 252/948 on GB, and the Plimptom PlimPad P60 came in at 339/1210. Is the Plimpad that much faster in the gHZ? Nope. Does it feel 20% faster - yup. Does it test 20% faster. Generally yes.

I mean don't take benchmarks for an end-all as ROMs and manufacturers tweak to get higher scores that don't translate into real world performance, but yeah, it's faster than my other tablets even accounting for I haven't bogged the thing down will all my apps yet.

For midgrade tablet, it's at the higher end in terms of processing performance. Where it starts to show budget is the camera. There's no way to sugar coat it, the camera or the processing software is somewhere around 2013-2016 quality. It's got the megapixels, but it's not got the quality. You know what, that's generally ok for a tablet. Are you planning on using it for a photo project? Probably not.

Next we come to the sound. I say bad things about the sound. It works. I wouldn't use it beyond what's required. I'd plan on headphones for the video streaming.

Memory is 6GB RAM and 128GB ROM. As of 2022 you've got space to install things, and you've got an OK amount of RAM to execute programs in. It's not a lot, but it's not too little. I'm sure by 2025 6GB of RAM will be considered scraping by but at the moment it's actually ok.

The OS actually received an update. I've dealt with so many no-name tablets and phones that what you buy is what you get that I am actually surprised. I don't know if it'll ever see another update, but it's good to know that the mechanism for Plimpton OS updates exists.

On the OS however there's something missing, or I'm failing to find it, and that's multi-user support. This tablet appears to ship for one person and one person only. I don't think that's a major problem for most, but my kids each have their own profiles on their devices and I have mine in the event I need to work off of their hardware (it's happened more than once.) Not seeing the standard Android multiuser there but then again it's been a bit since I was looking.

This unit is big and powerful enough that I'd really like to have profiles and be able to just slap it into someone's hands if needed.

The experience seems solid Google with maybe a little change in the launcher. I'm going to have to check what AOSP and Pixel were doing at Android 11 as it's not quite what the experience is in 13 at the moment. Nothing bad, just different.

The touch screen is ... I don't know how to put this but it's squeaky on the fingers. It's not a glass experience I'm used to. Not bad, just different. Like a lower slide coefficient or something with higher grain. You notice it when you glide type or swipe. Might just need to finger-oil it.

I realize I did not check to see if Netflix worked. I'll update the review if it doesn't. This has been an issue with several tablets and projectors. They do list it as downloadable, but that means nothing in the Netflix world.

7,000mAh battery, but runtime is closer to where I'd expect a 5000-5500 to be. Could just be because I'm hitting the unit pretty hard for the past few days. I'll update and remove this if the battery gets closer to where I'd expect (which it probably will when I stop being Mr Android Review Guy).

Overall - surprisingly acceptable tablet. Moderately dislike the speakers. Currently no complaints but will update the instant I get any.

title: Great, lacks water/drink carrying option, exterior pocket access
text:
I have a lot of tech backpacks at my house. I mean it's a surprising amount. Part of this has to do with going to CES for seven years, part of it has to do with having reviewed some for a tech blog back in the day. I needed a tech backpack for a project that I didn't have and this one seemed to fit the bill.

Lt's start off with as a method of carrying technology around this backpack fits a lot of the bills. Wire management, access to chargers, ways to separate tablets from laptops, it actually is a little bit overkill in the tech backpack department. It'll keep your tech dry, and it'll do exactly what you expect for protection (which is scratches and minor shock due to padding) - what it won't do is work as an all around backpack. What do I mean by that? Here ya go.

Part of all modern backpacks I've run across, especially ones that show people out hiking in the woods like this one does, is an external pocket for your water. External pockets for water, especially on a tech bag, are a must. You don't store water inside a mostly waterproof bag.

See those things that look like pockets on the bottom side of the bag where there should be pockets? They're not pockets. Do you see any rear access to attach a carabiner? If you do you've got better eyes than I do. So - no water bottle for you!

While this is well thought out to carry tech, it's notably missing random things most other bags I have have - safety whistle built into a snap? Nope. Carabiner access? Not really, or not evident. Reflective striping? Appears to be one thing that sets it out at night on the front and not on your back.

Oh side note - the image where it says "luggage strap" - just in case it's not clear - that's a strap that you can wrap around a luggage handle that sort of helps it hang out on top of luggage. The one strap means you need to pack the bag correctly. Two straps are on some bags, just if you travel a lot and don't pack well you'll want a two for.

It may sound like I'm coming down hard on this bag, I'm not. Two carabiner access points and an exterior pocket for a water bottle would make it a really great tech backpack. I mean, it is a really good one. Has managed to easily fight off a jelly spill, water spill, and keep everything in pretty decent shape so far. It is comfortable. Just lacking some basic backpack tech that could be solved without a major redesign.

title: Rear projection? I'd argue no. Square screen? Not so much. Fast assembly.
text:
I got this 100 inch screen because my 120 inch (different brand) projector screen was too large for me to handle and set up quickly (don't cry for me.)

It became an issue with a GS movie night when I ended up spending about 50 minutes putting up and taking down the other screen. It was time for something I could pop out and set up in no time because movie nights happen fairly regularly. That's why I chose this.

This unit appeared at first glance to be a pretty quick setup, and honestly it is. You can get this up and mostly wrinkle-free with the help of someone in about four minutes. You can do it by yourself in the same after you've played around a bit. But here's what drives me nuts:

Take a look at the pictures. Mine, other review I see, the top is bent. No matter how you rotate the poles that's gonna be bent slightly. Maybe it's just me, but man, that's all I can notice.

Next, this isn't rear projection capable. I mean, the screen fabric is. But you have to hang it from something. With what's included this means taking a cheap adhesive hook and I guess sticking it to your ceiling. You could purchase some string or something and tie it into a tree. I'd just stress it doesn't, as a stand, allow you to rear project unless you want the shadow of a pole dead center. My other screen does allow this.

What I consider real rear-projection screen / units have two poles - one left, one right, two tripods or feet. I mean, I've got to say center is quicker, but calling it rear projection.... technically yes. Can I rear project using what's included only? No. Maybe?

Now, what I want to know is why they're doing bag Inception. There's your carrying bag with a zipper, which opens up to reveal a carrying bag with a cinch, which opens up to reveal a projector screen bag, and a bag of accessories and grip grabby things that can also be turned into a sandbag.

Now, it may sound like I'm bashing this product. I'm not. I'd consider it slightly below average for an inexpensive projection screen, not rear projection capable, and so close to being great and just missing it. OK, those stick on hooks, I will bash them all the way to the manufacturer, those are terrible, but the thing itself is, overall, slightly below average but priced at the moment pretty decently.

It works, I can front project, I'm evidently the only person that gets annoyed by the slight bow at the top, I'll use my 120 inch two-feet projector when I've got time to set it up and this when I'm told I have to get an entire media setup and movie out into a field in an hour because plans went south.

This review has been edited by me as I started complaining about a velcro pole attachment and was wrong. I assembled the thing incorrectly twice because I'm just that awesome. If you don't see the large holes for the velcro straps to go in welcome to the club, you've assembled it the same way I did.

I can not stress enough how nice it is to be able to take this down quickly... rain, night, bugs, whatever all combine to make post-movie takedowns something you want done quickly.

title: 15 Amcrest units ordered, 4 dead, two of which are this model
text:
Where to start... the short and simple of this is I was tasked a couple of years ago with putting some rudimentary security in for an office building. This has been an ongoing project so we started with the same body style but slightly lower MP, same footprint as far as I can see.

We'll talk about the one pictured here in a minute. This one's not dead, just shipped without screws.

I placed one of these outside, water got in and ruined it, seal was breached. OK, cool, they sent me another one. Same thing happened and I was told that I needed to have the thing silicone attached to prevent water from getting on the back. OK, silicone attachment, torqued the thing down, five rains later water's in the unit. Talked to support again, they said the sideways mount I was using may be higher than IP 67 (immersion up to 1m depth) so mount it overhead. OK, I build an L-Bracket and it should not get anything but occasional side rain which can't be helped. Side of building, 25 feet up, birdhouse mounting tech, and it dies. This one I can't see water ingress, may have a straight up failure.

Decide to not go with this for outdoor use and use the outdoor cameras indoors. Looks a little strange, but meh they worked fine indoors. Purchased some outdoor cameras that appeared to actually be made for outdoors and since we're not using these for outdoors any more I went to install in office. So here's where this one comes into play - while configuring it I noticed it rebooted when I moved it, I should have stopped right then but I needed to get this camera in that day and... no.

On a ladder the contents of the camera come popping out at me. I attempt to push them in, short the thing, it reboots, short it again, try and come up with a solution as I have to get this done at this point. I look, there're 3 mounting points where there are supposed to be screws to hold the motherboard in. There are 0 screws installed. Not the wall anchor screws, not the bulb screws, motherboard screws missing.

I found a pair of eyeglass screws that I managed to make do as I had to get this done before labor day weekend. Tweeted at their support, no answer as of yet but it's labor day weekend so not particularly expecting one until Tuesday.

That said... picture quality is good, support site is lacking, they attempt to force you to register an email address to get firmware updates, auto firmware updates which the camera shows in settings never work. Some of the other cameras (same body, not all 4k) have been in operation for a couple of years now with no issues. I would not trust the IP rating they list. I'm sure it tested to those specs but when you put one outside in changing temperatures no.

Software appears to be a skinned Shenzhen OEM piece with logos and English. It works, but you'll probably want Blueiris or use an FTP.

So yeah, only hardware issue is water can get in them if there's not much side protection.

text:

title: Super Easy, Super Effective, but is missing USB-A
text:
This review is for the Phixero SATA-to-USB 3.0 for 2.5/3.5 inch drives. Which is also called (in the buttons) "SATA Adapter with Power Adapter." That is to say, the unit with a power adapter.

This is important. The product page has something like six options. You want THIS one if you're going to try to read data off of older drives or desktop drives, because those need the additional power.

So, on to the review...

The Phixero SATA for 3.5-inch drives is the most versatile SATA-to-USB converter I've seen, because it does something the others don't: It powers a 3.5" drive.

Small drives, the width of your cellphone, can be USB powered, but larger drives, like you may be pulling out of your desktop, are 3.5" and take too much power for a USB-powered adapter to drive. This converter includes a wall-wart to power the larger drives... and it works.

There is a wrinkle though - the power-in from the 12V power supply and the corresponding 12V input on the converter use a USB-C connector.

USB-C is 5 volts, not 12 volts, so this seems dangerous. Specifically, the power adapter is dangerous, if you plug it into another device.

With that out of the way, the other challenge is that this version, the powered version for larger hard drives, came with a USB-C end for the signal also, not the USB-A shown in the photo and there was no adapter in the box. I wasn't expecting this, and I've never seen a USB-C to USB-A converter. So that's a miss.

So... moving from the system I intended to use it with, which doesn't have any USB-C ports, to a laptop that does, I plugged it in.

Windows immediately recognized the USB "Mass Storage Device." Great!

I plugged in a drive I'd removed (after upgrading) from another system. Windows chimed and immediately recognized it, and made it fully readable. Complete win.

This converter is small, works flawlessly, doesn't require (at least for Windows) drivers, and does everything you'd expect. My only gripes are the power being 12 volts on USB-C and the data being USB-C without a USB-A adapter. So, as long as you're cautious and you have USB-C inputs, this is literally perfect.

The only thing I want to change is to get a paper-like screen protector. Even though I didn't spend much on this (less than my last Intuos, actually), I really wanna protect the screen. One thing to note: If you have a multi-monitor setup, you might need to get an HDMI to Displayport adapter. I needed to grab one so I could use this with my desktop with two other monitors as my HDMI was in use already. With my laptop, I just connected using the HDMI cable. Overall, I'm really excited to use this. Sculpting in Blender and drawing in Krita are amazing with the right tools.....And for a beginner (in terms of hardware), this is definitely the right tool. I can't believe I've been missing out on this for so long. Totally worth it.

title: Great for the price!
text:
[[VIDEOID:911fd5fefd4e83c12e601f428dc105b5]] Below is my review for the product as it was received.

Box was very obviously damaged in transit. Box was smashed and camera was loose in box. Figured I'd try it out anyway, but I've got really mixed thoughts.

Pro:
1. Hardware - This camera is the perfect size for a windshield mount. It is very small and very light. The buttons are placed in easy to access places. Mounting solution is extremely sturdy.
2. Audio - The audio is fantastic. Speaking at normal volume, the mic was able to pick up everything said in the vehicle. I wish I had kept the video with the recorded audio, but it really is great. I also have another dash cam that costs twice as much that has terrible audio in comparison.
3. Firmware - I could easily navigate the menu system without having to read a manual. The interface is very intuitive.
4. 1080p FHD - It does record at a decent resolution, but quality depends on the speed of the MicroSD card and quality of light. I had much better results recording at 720p. The viewing angle is also great and I was able to see vehicles to the side and all across intersections.
5. Auto-On/Off - This is the best. Automatically begins recording when your car is turned on and shuts off when your car is turned off.
6. Image stabilization - At this price range, I'm shocked this exists. It actually does a fantastic job of keeping the image stable.

Con:
1. Battery - does not keep charge for long. You'll definitely need to use the car adapter.
2. Low Light - Video in low-light or night is not crisp or clear, even after adjusting exposure.
3. File Naming - There doesn't seem to be any rhyme or reason to the way files are named. 00000001.AVI, 00050002.AVI, 00000005.AVI, Then in a different folder was 00050004.AVI...No clue.

Mixed:
1. Still images - Not terrible, but not great. It is nice to have this feature just in case.
2. Micro SD - Camera accepts MicroSD Class 4 or better. I tried it with 32GB up to 200GB and it functioned perfectly. File system needs to be FAT32. The camera can format the SD card in the camera. What makes the MicroSD a mixed bag....Well...The first time I stuck a card in, it ended up inside the camera instead of in the MicroSD slot. I had to open the device to get my card out...it was just chilling in the middle. Have to be very careful when placing card...make sure you're actually pushing it into the slot.

Final Thoughts:
For the price, this is a really good dash camera. It certainly beats the tar out of a few others I have tried. I wish the battery worked a bit longer (when it dies, all your settings vanish), but it should be fine as long as you keep it charged. Video is really good in the daytime. I'm happy with the quality. I also LOVE the audio is so clear. This company has some great microphones. The suction cup mechanism is also wonderful. It kept the camera in place and has a ball joint with excellent mobility. This is definitely going to be a permanent fixture in my wife's car.

It has everything a tech bag should have these days:

- removable portion that doubles as tablet-sized shoulder bag with strap

- another zippered side compartment (with waterproofing) to hold a small water bottle

I really wanted to like this bag more. Its attractive and has GREAT functionality. But for me - its missing several things that I personally need:

- rubber skids or a thin layer of leatherette on the bottom

Note that the removable external compartment leaves a zipper line on the bag exterior. Its not ugly, and is somewhat aesthetic in its implementation. And for me, the "lock" is feature that screams "this is for kids." As we grownups all know, a thief will just take the bag and slash it open.

So perhaps this is a GREAT bag for a school going teen.

Recommended! But if you bring a large water bottle with you to work every day, and you're serious about your water, look elsewhere.

title: We like the design - mostly - but are would prefer one modification
text:
Okay, so I grabbed this Hangcheng Smart Speaker Table Stand because my wife and I just bought an Apple Home Pod and I thought it would be a nice looking stand and help give us some great sound quality. So the heads up on this review is - we are being a bit picky and there are two "cons" we have that might be nothing for you. It really does deserve a 5 star in most way, but this these cons are just that much too off for us to go full 5.

It's a great looking stand and the metal material should last a good long time. The look overall - while arguably "modern" - should also fit into most rooms and decors. Meaning, it has a nice look and if you're already fine with putting one of these new types of technology into the room, this style of stand should also work for you.

So... the cons...
1. My wife had already reached down and plugged the Home Pod in by the time we got this Hangcheng Smart Speaker Table Stand and I'm being totally honest when I say we were being lazy and did not unplug it to see if we could fit the cord through the narrow slats of the Hangcheng Smart Speaker Table Stand. Nope, been a few days and still been lazy (read: busy) and haven't done it. Looking down there it seems the cord would attach from the plug part, so you probably could slip it between, but it is something to be aware of - again, we have the Apple Home Pod, so check with any other brands how the plug works and it you could slip it through. Otherwise, it lays over the top of the stand and tips the Home Pod forward. Again, we (most likely) will be able to pull the plug apart at the plug and slide it through - but a heads up on this. We call it a con because we have to now do it, if we want to move it quickly we won't be able to once it is through, and without having done it (for both above reasons) it looks a bit weird tipped over.

2. The point at which the Apple Home Pod sits on the stand - we would have preferred it was either sitting on that ring directly or there was a platform on which it would sit.

As it is designed, the Home Pod sits on the lower RING at a point in the lower side of the Home Pod, not the base, which is a flat portion of the Home Pod designed for it to sit on a table top.

The Home Pod outer material is a cloth of some kind and without actually testing to see if it'll happen, we are concerned that letting it sit on this ring would indent the ring into the material of the Home Pod. At this time, we don't wish to do that or test it and actually see our concern realized. We MIGHT get another Home Pod and not care with one and try it, we MIGHT not eventually care with this one, we MIGHT find another way of setting it on there by making our own "deck" for the Home Pod to sit on. Maybe we're just being overly cautious in wanting to care for the look of the expensive Home Pod we got. I mean, it's a nice gift to ourselves, so we don't want the outer material damaged.

We would have preferred a deck level the Home Pod can sit on within the stand - like on a table top, but within this nice looking stand - or that the ring sat fully under the Home Pod and formed a deck on the bottom, rather than the lower side of the Home Pod. I tried to show this in the photos.

In the end we do like the stand and we'll keep it, but at present, won't use it for the Home Pod. We might try to play with it, we might use it for something else. We don't know. But if you ARE concerned about that material on the outside of the Home Pod like we are, keep this design in mind. Also keep in mind your cord fitting. It is a great looking stand, but this one design alteration would be ideal.

title: Well designed, well constructed travel backpack
text:
My wife was not at all sure why I'd get another backpack or travel bag, but what drew me to this
ZOMFELT Carry On Backpack was the idea that it's a backpack (ease of carry), but opens and lays out like a suitcase (ease of packing/using/unpacking). When it arrived and we started to pick it apart she got it - and I was proved correct - this is a well designed bag.

Our trips tend to include a carry-on (though we travel by car) for our easy to get to stuff (think carry-on quickness). I like having a day's worth of items at hand and this ZOMFELT Carry On Backpack will work perfectly for that. Also, my wife does travel infrequently for work, so I knew it would be an easy-to-use bag for her. In the end we are both impressed and it has lived up to what I wanted and expected - simply by the images on the product page and other reviews.

So why do we like it?
1. It's a perfect size. Think backpack and you've pretty much got it. It has an expandable option to the sides to fill it fuller, but without that you've already got a great amount of room. Also in appearing as a backpack you're not advertising you're carrying all your clothes, etc.

2. It actually does not work (well) as a backpack. Because it is designed as a suitcase - opening fully and laying out - it really doesn't work overall as a backpack and for our needs, that's fine. We have backpacks, and have tried to use them as a travel bag, but never liked that the do not open fully and are always wanting to close. This gives us the ease of use of the backpack, but the easy access of a suitcase. But do keep this in mind - if you're wanting to simply open the top for access, that's not working here.

3. There are slots and pockets like a backpack, so you could bring work items and access those - mostly on the outside. Again, to get IN you'll open it from the side (mostly) like a suitcase, making it more difficult if full to access things in the way you would a backpack - hope that makes sense. Again, if you want a normal backpack, this isn't it. But for what we wanted, it's great. Now... back to the side slots and pockets. You could carry files, we THINK a laptop would do alright in the back slot - shoulder straps out - and we think you could keep it from getting crushed doing so. We did not try it. But you SHOULD BE ABLE to do that.

4. The inside compartment has a lot of room. If my wife is making a plane trip for even 2 - 3 days I should be able to pack what she needs. With the suitcase strap on the back she could put it on the extended handle of the suitcase and take both - but a quick trip, this would do.

5. It comes with 3 packing cubes: A main one for your clothes that would lay on the bottom, a small one with a large "window" for..., and a toiletry bag - which is decent, but we have far better toiletry bags we'd use of the same or similar size.

6. The materials and construction appear to be top notch. We always take zippers as a sign of quality and these are really good. The material for the bag is also nice, feels, nice, and should handle rain well. I'd say the "weak link" is the packing cubes, but the large one is still great and the middle size window one is pretty good, with only the toiletry bag feeling like it's "cheap," but as we have many, we're good there. I do like that it includes these and think such a detail is a bonus and start move.

In the end we really like this bag. I wanted something that could be a single, go-to bag for quick trips, an add on bag if we didn't need another one to support our suitcase(s), and something for ease of carry. This ZOMFELT Carry On Backpack gives us all of that. If we flew it would be our carry on. Taking a cruise? It's the bag we'd carry the first and last day "for just in case." It's a nice bag and we're happy to have it.

title: One nearly 4 foot tall speaker. Nice sound. No user instructions.
text:
[[VIDEOID:39a47248dba72bde6aed7278fa384f0a]] This speaker does not have user instructions, just a diagram of the back of the speaker and the remote control. Also, this speaker is BIG--nearly 4' tall (more accurately, 44" tall, 15.5" from front to back, and 14.25" wide)--and HEAVY (feels closer to 50 lbs. than the stated 25 lbs.). It does have handles on both sides and two handles on the top. Also, a pull-out handle so you can tilt and roll the speaker around on the small wheels embedded at the bottom edge. Still, you may want two people in order to safely lift the speaker into a car. This is probably the best sounding speaker in our house (from the bass to the treble). Even the lowest setting on the speaker can be heard throughout our entire house when using the Bluetooth function, but the LINE and USB inputs were softer.

The speaker comes with a WIRELESS MICROPHONE. It needs 2 AA batteries (not included). With the speaker on, just turn on the microphone and hit the Mic.Pri. button on the back of the speaker until you hear it. Talk away, even while the music is playing. The range of the wireless mic is about 40-45' from the speaker. You also get a REMOTE CONTROL that needs 2 AAA batteries (not included). It doesn't work that well unless you point it at the front, top area of the speaker. Even then, it's iffy--even when you're near the speaker. You also get a power cord. Plug the cord into the speaker and the electric outlet and wait some hours for the battery to fully change. A light indicates if it's charging (red) or full (green). I charged it overnight, so I only know that it took more than 4 hours. You can unplug and play for hours off of just the battery power.

The LED LIGHTS illuminate the front of the speaker and also come out of the ball on top to play across the ceiling. The ball on top isn't very flashy unless you have a ceiling to see the projected lights. The lights patterns change in time to the beat when the music is loud, or even when someone taps on the top of the speaker.

To use the BLUETOOTH function, hit the Mode button on the speaker until the not-the-Line-or-the-FM-option comes up. Search for the BeFree on your Bluetooth enabled computer, tablet, phone, etc. to pair as usual. It was easy to do. The Bluetooth range is over 30' between the device and the speaker. The speaker plays what your device is playing. Switch the Mode to FM, extend the antenna, and hit the scan button on the remote to find the stations. You can then flip through the stations. It only picked up 4 of the stations in my area, and only one of those was clear enough to listen to.

You can insert a SD card and hit the record button to record the audio. There is also a playback button on the remote. I've not been able to get this to work. If you connect a MP3 player, phone, etc. using the USB port, it will simply charge the device for you. Customer service explained, "The only way you are able to play audio through the USB port is by plugging in a USB flash driver with pre-loaded audio." I was able to do this. Also, "...you can only connect a device (phone, MP3 player, iPod, iPad, laptop) with an audio cable (unit must be in LINE IN mode) to play any audio." I was able to do this with my iPod using the included cord that plugs into the headphone plug on your device and into the R/L spot on the back of the speaker.

On the speaker, you can control the overall volume, treble volume, bass volume, and echo. You can plug in one microphone, one guitar, and control the volume of each. There is an optional DC charging input on the back. There are two LINE IN (Right and Left plugs for each) like the type on old-style VCRs.

So, do I like this speaker? Well, it's nice. But as a single woman, I find it hard to move around. And I wanted full INSTRUCTIONS so I could fully use the thing. I bugged Customer Service until they answered my questions, and I passed some of that information on in this review.

UPDATE: I drove this to my church for use during an afternoon "fun day" outdoors. It was very convenient to not have to plug this in. We rolled the speaker around to parking lot based on where the games were. The kids loved the lights. We played music through Bluetooth, and the music volume was turned up so it could be heard across the property. The music sounded good even when this loud.

title: Very stiff joints.
text:
Hello,
I hope you can understand my written description and my photos. Sorry for the long winded review.
This is the first tv mount that we have installed, and it’s on a 32 inch tv.
I chose this model because it said full range, and the way our master bedroom is set up, the tv is in the sitting area, but you can’t see it from the bed.
I wanted a mount that would extend out, and be able to turn the tv around by about 120 to 180 degrees.
This mount has an “up” side...meaning that you can only install it one way, so it’s range of motion is not equal on both sides as the arm starts its extension from the wall on the left side, and not in the middle (this could easily be eliminated if you could get the arm assembly bars off and reverse them, so that you could install the unit upside down, but you cannot.). They are 1/4 round at the top, and square at the bottom, and the caps at the end don’t come off. So although you can loosen them, there are only two holes anyway, and the caps prevent them from being removed.
The install itself is pretty unremarkable and they give you plenty of tools (although their spanner/wrench was the wrong size). It’s sort of irrelevant anyway, as you won’t be able to put those big screws in the wall with a little skinny 3 inch wrench.
Ok, so the next thing (which is not this company’s fault), but you do need to be aware of...make sure your tv screw holes are definitely more than 4 inches apart. Otherwise you will have to set the tv on the stand off center like I did. Although, if you kad a large tv, this may not be a noticeable issue.
My tv is 32 inches, so not big.
In order to 1. Attach the tv to the stand and 2. Be able to see it from the bed, we had to attach it off center. Now, there are two bars showing from the side of the tv (this could have been avoided if they’d put a few extra holes in the arm assembly so that we could slide the arms and the tv over).
The other thing that I want you to be aware of, is that the joints in this wall mount stand are exceedingly stiff, like they need spraying with WD40, or somehow loosening.
I’m keeping the item because I got it on a 50% off lightening deal, and it “works” for me because I rarely watch the tv in bed anyway.
However, had I have purchased this at a local store or for somewhere that needed more use or was in a communal area, I’d definitely be returning it!

title: I CAN NOW SEE THE WILDLIFE WHILE HIKING
text:
My dog and I spend quite a bit a time hiking on a nature preserve that is near our house. The last few years as I age I have noticed that my eyesight is not as good as it used to be. My dog , boxer loves to go out looking at deer, turkey rabbits, well anything actually, but those are the things he really likes to watch for. It is really quite amazing because when he sees something he just immediately stops and watches. He never makes a sound or moves. title: Fantastic Image
text:
This new projector is great. I'm replacing an Epson 705HD with it. The 705HD is a 720p resolution projector, this Home Cinema 1440 is 1080p – the difference in resolution is night and day. The project produces a very crisp and sharp image. And the illumination is greatly increased too, nearly twice that of the 705HD. Even during daytime with the blinds open the projected image is bright.

Some things that I like that want to comment on, number one is the ease of setup. Just straight out of the box using the default setting the unit preformed great. The auto keystone feature (Screen Fit) makes it a snap to adjust the image when the unit is set off to the side. I also tried out the Quick Corner setup and that was nearly just as easy – it gets you close and you only have to slightly adjust the one corner. Epson had pretty much made the setup of this projector within the capability of even the most novice of users.

Connectivity has been improved too. There is just about every connection that you might ever need for a variety of connection scenarios, and you get two of some. Connections in consist of a network connection (LAN), USB-A, USB-B, 2x Computer, 2x HDMI, and Composite Video/Audio (RCA). There is also a monitor out port. The one and only thing missing (and that the 705HD has) is a S-Video input. I've experimented with hooking up a number of different video sources – video players (DVD/Blu-ray), game systems (PlayStation, Xbox, Wii, Dreamcast), and computer (laptop). I even plugged in my older Kindle Fire HD 7 (the one with them micro-HDMI port). Everything worked perfect. I do sort of miss having the S-Video port as I still have a laserdisc player that I use on occasion – but I was still able to connect that up using a conversion box that upscale the S-Video to HDMI.

Another thing that I liked is the remote. I like what I consider full-sized remotes, and dislike those small credit-card sized remotes. The remote that comes with the 1440 is full-sized and has regular sized buttons. Makes it very easy to find the buttons that you need (least for me).

One thing I might mention about the differences between the two units. The Home Cinema 1440 is quite a bit bigger than the 705HD (see photo I posted). That wasn't an issue with me, I have space to accommodate the bigger unit, but it might be an issue with someone else.

Like most of these projectors this unit has a fan – the sound level of the fan is about the same as the other projector. It's not really noticeable unless you're focusing on listening to it. There is an air filter for the fan. The instruction manual mentions that it should be cleaned occasionally with a vacuum and the manual gives a part number if it ever needs to be replace.

Overall, I'm totally impressed with this projector – the image quality, the level of luminance, the connectivity. I seriously can't think of what you might need to make this better. I whole heartily recommend this projector.
